abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic inflammatory central nervous system (CNS) disease. Although current immunotherapies control relapses, they have limited impact on progression, which might reflect incomplete access to or modulation of compartmentalized CNS inflammation. Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells can infiltrate tissues, but their ability to access and eliminate immune cells residing in the CNS remains elusive. We report the treatment of five individuals with progressive or relapsing-remitting MS with autologous CD19 CAR T cells to assess safety-relevant aspects, CNS bioavailability, and compartment-specific effects. The intervention induces remodeling of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) B cell pool, with a sustained reduction in CSF humoral biomarkers. Notably, CSF-infiltrating CAR T cells selectively upregulate phosphodiesterase 7B, while reconstituted peripheral B cells show altered cytokine and homing profiles. These findings indicate compartment-specific immunomodulation beyond peripheral B cell depletion and support controlled trials to test safety, durability, and efficacy.
title: CD19 CAR T cell therapy alters disease-associated immune signatures in multiple sclerosis

abstract: RNA viruses form membraneless condensates in host cells to drive replication, but whether these compartments regulate host RNAs remains unclear. Using multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (MERFISH)-based subcellular transcriptomics, we quantified cellular mRNA recruitment into Ebola virus condensates under basal and interferon (IFN)-stimulated states. We find that, in the basal state, cellular RNAs with minimally folded coding regions are selectively recruited. Under IFN stimulation, however, IFN-stimulated genes (ISGs) with structured 3' UTRs concentrate in viral condensates. We find that both RNA structural features are conserved in the viral genome and support its retention in condensates. In parallel, for cellular mRNAs, we find that partitioning into condensates prolongs RNA half-life and amplifies, rather than dampens, ISG expression. Fruit bats, which do not experience severe disease from RNA viruses, instead have ISGs with reduced 3' UTR folding and may evade condensate sequestration, thus enabling balanced antiviral responses. This selective stabilization links condensate function to RNA regulation as a molecular determinant of virus-host co-evolution and disease pathogenesis.
title: RNA folding drives species-dependent host mRNA partitioning in Ebola virus condensates

abstract: Understanding respiratory virus transmission requires integrating pathogen genomic data with detailed epidemiological context. We analyzed >85,000 SARS-CoV-2 genomes linked to epidemiological data collected in Massachusetts from November 2021 to January 2023. Collected in 666 settings, including schools, colleges, and skilled nursing facilities, this dataset enabled direct comparison of within-setting transmission to community-wide risk. Elevated transmission was concentrated in specific age-defined subpopulations-older adolescents in schools, undergraduates in colleges, and residents in nursing facilities-with little additional risk among other groups, notably including staff. Young adults, particularly in colleges, played a disproportionate role in spread, and new viral lineages consistently expanded first within this group. Viral spread followed reproducible urban-to-rural gradients, and vaccination was associated with reduced onward transmission. We further estimated sequencing thresholds required for timely detection of emerging variants. Together, these findings reveal consistent demographic and spatial structure in SARS-CoV-2 transmission that can inform viral respiratory pathogen genomic surveillance.
title: Genomic surveillance reveals age-structured SARS-CoV-2 transmission across settings

abstract: Large and giant DNA viruses that infect unicellular eukaryotes are abundant in the environment but have rarely been found in the gut microbiome. The discovery of such viruses that prevail in the digestive system of humans and animals exposes a long-overlooked facet of the gut microbiome that clarifies the origin of poxviruses. Newly discovered viruses distributed in animal digestive systems are the closest known relatives of the clade containing smallpox virus.
title: Poxviruses probably evolved in the digestive system of animals

abstract: Algal blooms are important ecological phenomena that drive carbon fixation and fuel the marine food web. Viral infection often ends them abruptly. Some bacteria can sense infected algal cells and then act in synergy with viruses to expedite a bloom’s collapse.
title: Bacteria and viruses team up to hasten the demise of algal blooms

abstract: Homo erectus represents one of the longest-persisting hominin species, with a geographic range from Africa to eastern Eurasia from approximately 1.9 million years ago 1 to 108 thousand years ago (ka) 2 . Despite this, there are still large gaps in our understanding of the adaptation capabilities of this species and the extent of its persistence in China. Assumptions over ecological preferences based on the Trinil 3 , Sangiran 4 and Ngandong 2 (in Java) open woodland–grassland mosaics have persisted, combined with limited direct stable carbon isotope measurements in Asia. Here we present a rich temporal and environmental context for nine hominin teeth, eight of which were morphologically and genetically identified as H. erectus 5 , found in two sister caves in Guangxi province, southern China. We modelled 43 radiometric ages from five dating techniques to establish a timeline for H. erectus presence in this region. Stable and clumped isotopes and trace elements from teeth were used to establish the dominant environments and their behavioural responses. We show that H. erectus was present in southern China between 324 and 184 ka, which is substantially more recent than previously established in this region for unequivocally H. erectus fossils at approximately 400 ka. The evidence suggests that they were persisting in closed rainforest ecosystems, thought to be the domain of only Homo sapiens , and were demonstrating long-term mobility and ecological flexibility. This evidence challenges the assumptions over the ecological preferences and behavioural limitations of H. erectus .
title: Rainforest adaptation in late Homo erectus from southern China

abstract: A major goal in neuroscience is to map the transformation of information as it flows through the brain. For example, neurons at many levels of the visual hierarchy are attuned to motion direction1–5. However, links between motion-selective computations and cell types at various stages of the visual hierarchy remain unidentified. A key first step in delineating these relationships is to map the wiring diagrams that connect different motion-selective cell types. Here we establish a systematic, cell-type-specific circuit-mapping method, combining an anterograde trans-neuronal fluorescent tracer (mWGA–mCherry)6 with spatial transcriptomics (multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (MERFISH))7,8 to establish TransA-MERFISH. We used TransA-MERFISH to comprehensively map the synaptic target cell types of four retinal ganglion cell subclasses in superior colliculus (SC) at cell-type resolution. These experiments unexpectedly revealed that retinal on–off direction-selective ganglion cells (ooDSGCs) innervate several direction-selective SC cell types, but do not innervate a SC cell type that was previously reported to display strong direction-selective responses. We validated these results using orthogonal approaches and demonstrated the sensitivity and specificity of TransA-MERFISH. Functional studies of SC activity before and after ablation of retinal direction-selective circuits confirmed that these computationally distinct, ooDSGC-dependent and -independent direction-selective cell types are commingled in SC. Together, our study establishes TransA-MERFISH as a robust framework for mapping wiring diagrams at the cell-type level and uncovers divergent computational mechanisms of motion detection in early visual processing. TransA-MERFISH combines anterograde trans-neuronal tracing and spatial transcriptomics and reveals distinct retinal on–off direction-selective ganglion cell-dependent and independent motion-selective pathways in superior colliculus, establishing a sensitive cell-type-resolved framework for wiring-diagram reconstruction in early visual processing.
title: TransA-MERFISH reveals divergent post-retinal direction-selective circuits

abstract: Current understanding of the host tissue response to solid tumours is largely based on investigations of tumour types in isolation 1 . Given the breadth and diversity of human tumour pathology and contributions of tumour microenvironment (TME) cells to disease progression, pan-cancer analysis is needed to bridge major themes of stromal and immune cell evolution. To date, however, efforts to compare the TME response across cancers have been limited in scope 2 , 3 . Here we conduct a comprehensive pan-cancer analysis by algorithmically screening thousands of publicly available single-cell transcriptomic datasets for stromal and immune signatures across species and tissue types. We demonstrate conserved hallmarks of host cell transcriptional programming in response to malignancy across 42 cancer types in more than 2,000 human and mouse tumour samples. These findings are codified as an interactive web atlas ( tmeatlas.stanford.edu ) and software package (scTME) that will serve as practical resources for the systematic interrogation of the TME in tumours.
title: Conservation of the tumour microenvironment across organs and species

abstract: Hominin fossils and genetic evidence indicate that several hominin populations occupied East and Southeast Asia during the Middle and Late Pleistocene epoch1–10. Homo erectus fossils remain scarce in southern China and mainland Southeast Asia4,8,11. Here we report nine newly discovered late Middle Pleistocene hominin teeth from the Naxian and Baxian caves at the Chongzuo study area, Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, southern China, dated to around 324–184 thousand years ago12. Palaeoproteomics reveals the presence of an endogenous dental proteome in all five hominin teeth studied molecularly. Four teeth contain a derived H. erectus substitution in ameloblastin that to date has been observed only in older Middle Pleistocene H. erectus specimens from China13. The proteomes of these four teeth differ from the previous H. erectus proteomes from China at another ameloblastin position, suggesting that these specimens represent a previously unsampled H. erectus population. Morphometric and geometric morphometric methods support an attribution of these teeth to H. erectus, as well as four additional teeth. This fills a gap in the geographical and chronological distribution of H. erectus in East Asia. The fifth tooth studied proteomically, PA1796, is morphologically distinct from H. erectus, Neanderthals (Homo neanderthalensis) and modern humans (Homo sapiens), and does not contain the H. erectus-derived amino acid sequence. The late survival of H. erectus on mainland East Asia suggests that at least two hominin lineages, H. erectus and Homo longi (Denisovans)6,7, possibly represented by PA1796, were present in the region towards the end of the Middle Pleistocene, with the first documented occurrence of H. sapiens not much later5. Late Middle Pleistocene hominin teeth from the Naxian and Baxian caves of southern China, dated to around 324–184 thousand years ago, fill a gap in the geographical and chronological distribution of Homo erectus in East Asia.
title: Evidence for late Middle Pleistocene Homo erectus in mainland East Asia

Here we present HypoAD, an atlas of the human hypothalamus in ageing and AD, including high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging from 458 individuals and single-nucleus RNA sequencing of 614,403 nuclei from young participants, patients with AD and age-matched non-dementia control participants. We show that hypothalamic subregions governing metabolism, stress and circadian rhythms are particularly vulnerable, showing notable changes in both volumes and gene expression during ageing and AD. At the molecular level, machine learning models identified the inflammatory response and regulators of circadian rhythms as key cellular predictors of AD. These signatures were reflected in specific cell types: microglia transitioned to a pro-inflammatory state, whereas inhibitory neurons within sleep-regulating and circadian-regulating hypothalamic subregions showed the most profound transcriptional alterations, including disruptions in ligand-receptor interactions and G-protein-coupled receptor signalling. HypoAD provides a high-resolution volumetric map and a transcriptomic atlas of the human hypothalamus in ageing and AD, relating lifestyle and behavioural changes to the relevant volumetric and molecular pathways. In addition, HypoAD provides a framework to investigate hypothalamic dysfunction and establishes a roadmap for targeted interventions aimed at mitigating physiological disruptions to potentially slow disease progression.
title: Hypothalamic volume and cell-type changes in ageing and Alzheimer’s disease

abstract: MethodsIn this phase 2, randomized, controlled trial, we assigned participants with rifampin-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis to receive the standard four-drug combination (isoniazid–rifampin–pyrazinamide–ethambutol; HRZE) for 24 weeks; bedaquiline–delamanid–moxifloxacin for 16 weeks; or one of 10 new four-drug combinations for 16 weeks. The new regimens contained ganfeborole, BTZ-043, or both, with combinations of bedaquiline, delamanid, moxifloxacin, pyrazinamide, pretomanid, and linezolid. The primary end point was the log10(time to positivity) slope (rate of change from baseline to week 12 in the time to Mycobacterium tuberculosis growth in a positive sputum culture). The treatment effect was assessed as the Bayesian posterior probability of superiority of each new regimen to HRZE with respect to the primary end point (results were used to select regimens for further evaluation, rather than for characterization of efficacy). ResultsA total of 401 participants underwent randomization; 371 were included in the modified intention-to-treat population and 400 in the safety population. We identified two promising regimens for further evaluation: ganfeborole–bedaquiline–pretomanid–moxifloxacin (BPMG) and BTZ-043–bedaquiline–delamanid–moxifloxacin (BDMT). The log10(time to positivity) slope was 0.129 log10(days) per week (95% Bayesian credible interval, 0.112 to 0.146) with BPMG and 0.142 log10(days) per week (95% Bayesian credible interval, 0.126 to 0.160) with BDMT, as compared with 0.118 log10(days) per week (95% Bayesian credible interval, 0.105 to 0.131) with HRZE, for a relative difference of 9.1% (95% Bayesian credible interval, −8.6 to 29.0) and 20.5% (95% Bayesian credible interval, 2.7 to 41.1), respectively, and a posterior probability of superiority of 0.83 and 0.99. The incidence of adverse events of grade 3 or higher was 38% in the BPMG group (none of the participants discontinued), 28% in the BDMT group (one discontinued because of a drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms), and 24% in the HRZE group (none discontinued). Bedaquiline–moxifloxacin–pyrazinamide–BTZ-043 was discontinued because of hepatotoxic effects. ConclusionsIn this trial, two four-drug regimens, one with ganfeborole and one with BTZ-043, showed evidence of potential efficacy and a safety profile that did not preclude progression to further evaluation. (Funded by Innovative Medicines Initiative 2 Joint Undertaking and others; PARADIGM4TB ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT06114628.)
title: Assessing Multiple Treatment Regimens for Tuberculosis

abstract: Ribosome-associated quality control (RQC) ensures proteostasis by actively degrading aberrant translation intermediates on stalled ribosomes, yet its physiological role in gene regulation remains elusive. Here, we demonstrate that Drosophila circadian clocks employ RQC to sustain 24-h behavioral rhythms. RNA interference-mediated depletion of RQC components in circadian pacemaker neurons impaired free-running locomotor rhythms. In particular, the loss of Caliban ( Clbn ) function in clearing 60S-associated faulty polypeptides led to weak but long-period rhythms in adult locomotor activity. These behavioral phenotypes were accompanied by delayed accumulation of the core clock protein PERIOD (PER), most evidently in pigment-dispersing factor-expressing clock neurons, and dampened structural plasticity of their axons. per heterozygosity exaggerated CLBN depletion-induced period lengthening, whereas overexpression of the PER-associating factor TIMELESS blunted this effect. Clbn deficiency in Drosophila S2R+ cell cultures increased the generation of prematurely terminated PER species, particularly when PER translation is high, and sensitized full-length PER to phosphorylation-dependent decay. These findings support PER as a clock-relevant RQC substrate, providing a mechanistic link between translation flux, co-translational surveillance, and circadian timekeeping.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Co-translational surveillance of nascent polypeptides times circadian rhythms in Drosophila

abstract: Humans can pursue a near-infinite variety of tasks, but typically can only pursue a small number at the same time. We hypothesize that humans leverage experience on one task to preemptively learn solutions to other tasks that were accessible but not pursued. We formalize this idea as "Multitask Preplay", an algorithm that replays experience on one task as the starting point for "preplay"-counterfactual simulation of an accessible but unpursued task. Preplay is used to learn a predictive representation that can support fast, adaptive task performance later on. When implemented within deep reinforcement learning, it predicts human generalization to novel tasks more accurately than traditional planning and predictive representation methods across grid-worlds and a 2D Minecraft domain. Additionally, Multitask Preplay improves an artificial agent's ability to generalize to new environments sharing task co-occurrence structure. These findings demonstrate that Multitask Preplay is a scalable theory of human counterfactual learning and generalization; endowing artificial agents with this capacity can significantly improve their performance in challenging multitask environments.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Preemptive solving of future problems: Multitask Preplay in humans and machines

abstract: Multi-principal element alloys are promising structural materials for nuclear, aerospace, and fusion applications, yet their accelerated discovery is limited by the prohibitive cost of evaluating point-defect transport and self-healing behavior across vast compositional spaces. Here, we establish local lattice distortion (LLD), an intrinsic feature of chemically complex alloys, as a predictive and universal descriptor for vacancy–interstitial diffusivity convergence. We develop and validate a high-fidelity machine-learning interatomic potential based on the moment tensor potential formalism for body-centered-cubic Zr–Ti–Nb alloys, enabling accurate large-scale simulations of defect energetics and migration. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal a robust inverse correlation between LLD and the activation energy disparity between vacancies and interstitials. This relationship is further validated in face-centered-cubic V–Co–Ni and Ni–Pd systems, demonstrating transferability across distinct chemistries and crystal structures. LLD-induced narrowing of vacancy–interstitial mobility differences promotes Frenkel pair recombination and defect self-healing. Mechanistically, vacancy diffusion is governed by the energy barrier associated with bond-length compression at the saddle state, together with statistical sampling of low-barrier jumps mediated by oversized atoms. These findings establish lattice distortion as a powerful, physically grounded design lever that links nanoscale disorder to point-defect self-healing, offering a practical pathway for the accelerated discovery of next-generation structural materials for extreme environments.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Harnessing lattice distortion for point-defect self-healing in multi-principal element alloys

abstract: Complex adaptive traits often comprise interacting, coevolving phenotypes that together for a syndrome that is shaped by multiple genetic loci. While using intraspecific variation is an established approach for investigating syndromes, such polymorphism typically captures only a subset of syndrome traits. Diapause, an alternative developmental pathway that evolved independently in many species to synchronize life cycles with resource availability, exemplifies this challenge. While subsets of this essential phenotype have long been studied at a single species level, the genomic basis of the full diapause syndrome remains poorly understood. This paucity of insights has fueled a long-standing debate about how life cycle synchronization evolves and whether convergent phenotypes employ shared mechanisms. Using a comparative genomic analysis spanning diverse diapause transitions in butterflies, we identified a large network of coevolving genes unique to diapausing species. The network is composed of functional modules spanning circadian regulation, metabolism, and cell cycle control. We tested whether this macroevolutionary scale network predicts microevolutionary dynamics, hypothesizing that this network is the polygenic architecture underlying the diapause syndrome. Analyses revealed that allelic variation in the diapause network is significantly enriched in signatures of local adaptation across latitudes, but only in diapausing species. Thus, we empirically show that diapause evolves through modular, coevolving gene networks, components of which impact intraspecific variation in diapause. Using this integrative perspective on a complex phenotype opens a horizon of inquiry for understanding seasonal adaptation across evolutionary scales, while demonstrating the power of integrating comparative genomics with microevolutionary dynamics to dissect complex phenotypic syndromes.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Coevolving gene networks underlying a phenotypic syndrome revealed via integrating comparative genomic and microevolutionary analyses

abstract: Cells utilize phase separation to compartmentalize biochemical reactions within biomolecular condensates. Although these compartments can enhance reaction rates by concentrating reactants, how they modulate kinetics beyond mass-action effects remains poorly understood. Here, using spontaneous protein ligation as a model reaction, we examined how the physicochemical microenvironment within condensates modulates reaction kinetics. We systematically analyzed condensates formed by folded PRM–SH3 scaffolds and intrinsically disordered proteins (LAF, TAF, and FUS). We designed a proximity-sensitive client probe to assess excluded-volume-driven increases in effective reactant concentration. In parallel, we characterized condensate hydrophilicity and associated changes in water activity, identifying these properties as additional key kinetic determinants. Together, our findings elucidate how effective concentration and hydrophilicity jointly regulate biochemical reactions within condensates.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Physicochemical microenvironments within biomolecular condensates govern reaction kinetics beyond mass-action effects

abstract: Windblown dunes are found everywhere in the Solar System where a supply of loose sediment is mobilized by gas flows, from the sluggish winds of Venus to speed-of-sound sublimation flows on comets. Their abundance is nontrivial because dunes only form where grains hop ballistically (“saltate”). This implies that winds across the Solar System reach “goldilocks” speeds that are just right to initiate and maintain saltation of whatever sediment is available despite vast variations in material and fluid properties, and gravity. Based on select observations, it was proposed that dune fields may be characterized by a near-threshold transport state where dune-forming winds minimally exceed the saltation threshold on Earth. Here, we demonstrate that this is indeed the case globally. Next, we show that, unlike riverbeds—which evolve to a similar state through adjustments of channel geometry—dune fields are born in it due to the rapid decrease in wind frequency with increasing wind speed. These results imply that grain sizes in windblown dunes provide a robust record of formative winds, such that corresponding wind speeds can be estimated from aeolian sandstones and dune deposits across planets. The near-threshold state of windblown dunes thus opens a promising line of investigation for paleoenvironmental and paleoclimate reconstructions on Earth and beyond.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Windblown dunes are born in sand at the brink of transport

abstract: Caveolae are 50 to 100 nm sized plasma membrane invaginations involved in cellular lipid uptake and lipid accumulation. Several caveolin1 and cavin1 mutations are associated with human lipodystrophy. Previous research identified caveolae proteins at lipid droplets, although their specific cellular function at lipid droplets is not understood. Here, we show that extracellular dietary lipids like oleic acid and cholesterol shift caveolae at the plasma membrane to highly spherical invaginations and induce the internalization of caveolin1. Within 3 h of lipid treatment, caveolin1 accumulates specifically to lipid droplets. Correlative fluorescence Focused Ion Beam - Scanning Electron Microscopy and split-APEX proteomics revealed that this localization occurs in the absence of intact caveolar vesicles but caveolin1 alone. Mechanistically, caveolin1 trafficking to lipid droplets is regulated by EHD2 at the plasma membrane, is dynamin independent, and proceeds via EEA1- and Rab5-positive endosomes within 1 h of oleic acid treatment. Lipid droplet accumulation of caveolin1 is independent of lysosomal activity. Functionally, caveolin1-enriched lipid droplets exhibit a significant increase in size, demonstrating that caveolin1 is critical for lipid droplet growth. Notably, the deletion of the central caveolin1 β-barrel (Cav1-F160X), a mutation identified in lipodystrophy patients, abolished caveolin1 lipid droplet trafficking and lipid droplet growth. Taken together, our results show that dietary lipids trigger caveolin1 internalization and accumulation at lipid droplets and a caveolin1-dependent lipid droplet growth, thereby providing an initial mechanistic basis for the lipodystrophic phenotype associated with caveolin1 mutations.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Lipid-induced Caveolin1 lipid droplet trafficking is associated with lipid droplet growth

abstract: The last decade has brought renewed interest to microbial influences on host biology, yet the roles of microbes in host reproductive biology are underappreciated and often defined by a profound maternal bias. This perspective synthesizes emerging evidence across the tree of life to highlight the paternal microbiome as an overlooked driver of fitness, reproductive output, and intergenerational health, impacting epigenetic sculpting of the sperm and embryo, sexual transmission of microbes, and male gamete functions. These contributions indicate that mating can involve interactions between holobionts rather than simply the union of the maternal and paternal genomes. Thus, uniting male reproduction with the growing generalizations of microbial symbiosis guides several conceptual, theoretical, and empirical avenues for research in the life sciences.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: The microbial world of male reproduction

abstract: As animal hosts adapted to land, Enterococcus species diverged from a common ancestor shared with Vagococcus species by acquiring genes essential for survival and transmission in the exposed arid environment. In addition to their intrinsic ruggedness, human-associated enterococci now frequently exhibit multidrug resistance, largely driven by the accumulation of antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) on mobile genetic elements (MGEs). However, the source of these resistance elements, their diversity in natural reservoirs, and their risks remain unclear. To investigate clinically relevant ARGs and their associated MGEs in a wastewater-impacted environment, we examined environmental vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE) recovered from a polluted urban river in Hanoi, Vietnam. Whole-genome sequencing of VRE isolates revealed multidrug-resistance pELF-type linear plasmids harboring a fluoroquinolone resistance gene ( qrtA ) encoding a major facilitator superfamily transporter. The qrtA gene appears to have originated on Vagococcus -related chromosomes and may have been mobilized by IS 1216E -associated MGEs. Vagococcus genomes show strong associations between ARGs, IS 1216E, and plasmids related to those in enterococci, and conjugation experiments demonstrated that pELF-type linear plasmids can transfer between Enterococcus and Vagococcus without major fitness costs. Comparative analysis of pELF-type linear plasmids, together with database mining, identified qrtA -positive clinical isolates from geographically separated regions in Asia and Europe, indicating that qrtA is not confined to a single local setting. These findings highlight the need for coordinated international One Health surveillance of ARG and MGE dynamics, including emerging determinants such as qrtA , together with interventions to limit their spread.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Linear plasmids mediate antimicrobial resistance gene transfer between environmental bacteria and hospital-adapted enterococci

abstract: Staphylococcus aureus extracts hemin from human hemoglobin (Hb) to overcome host-imposed iron limitation. How it recovers Hb-bound hemin from the hemoglobin:haptoglobin (Hb:Hp) complex, the major circulating form of Hb outside red blood cells, remains unclear. Here, we use cryo-electron microscopy, biophysical measurements, and solution kinetics to define how the S. aureus IsdH surface receptor extracts hemin from Hb:Hp. A 3.1 Å cryo-EM structure of Hb:Hp bound by full-length IsdH reveals that its N-terminal NEAT domain (N1) anchors it to αHb, whereas its downstream N2N3 extraction unit engages βHb to remove its hemin. The receptor engages Hb:Hp differently than isolated Hb, because N-linked glycans on haptoglobin bias the extraction unit toward βHb, sterically occluding its access to αHb while still permitting engagement by N1. Kinetic assays show that IsdH actively accelerates hemin release from Hb:Hp. Three-dimensional variability analysis indicates that this likely occurs via a dynamic interface in which receptor motions reposition the extraction unit relative to βHb, collectively supporting a model in which IsdH transiently perturbs the F-helix to promote hemin extraction. Alignment of that model with a previously determined CD163:Hb:Hp structure shows how IsdH may disrupt Hb:Hp recognition by macrophage and monocyte CD163 receptors, helping to explain how it may hinder clearance of Hb:Hp from circulation. In aggregate, these results help define the structural basis for hemin extraction from Hb:Hp and how IsdH may subvert receptor-mediated clearance of the Hb:Hp complex.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Cryo-EM provides insight into how the Staphylococcus aureus IsdH receptor removes hemin from the hemoglobin:haptoglobin complex

abstract: Lipid 1256 (L1256) is a large complex aminolipid produced by members of the phylum Bacteroidota that is formed by addition of a phosphatidic acid (PA) moiety to the precursor aminolipid, L654. Studies have shown that L1256 is enriched in diseased gingival tissues, linking synthesis of this aminolipid to sites of chronic inflammation. Given that PA is involved in membrane rearrangements and L654 is a known Toll-like receptor 2 ligand associated with health, we hypothesized that synthesis of L1256 could influence outer membrane vesicle (OMV) biogenesis and innate immune responses. Here, PG1647 was identified as a lipid synthase required for biosynthesis of L1256 in Porphyromonas gingivalis . Loss of PG1647 abolished L1256 and related minor species, while impairing membrane stress resistance and intracellular survival. PG1647 loss also increased OMV production and enhanced the proinflammatory activity of bacterial cells and OMVs. These phenotypes occurred without broad transcriptional changes, supporting lipid remodeling as a central driver. Structural and biochemical analyses supported a phospholipase D-like role for PG1647. Complementation with the Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron homologue BT3978 restored L1256 production in P. gingivalis and partially rescued associated phenotypes, suggesting functional conservation among the host-associated Bacteroidota . Additional studies determined that many species in the phylum Bacteroidota carry a similar functional enzyme, further indicating the importance of this class of enzyme for Bacteroidota’s physiological functions. Altogether, these findings show that loss of PG1647 alters OMV biogenesis, inflammatory activity, and host-associated fitness in the endogenous oral pathogen, P. gingivalis , linking these phenotypic changes to PG1647-dependent aminolipid remodeling.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Serine–glycine lipid homeostasis in Bacteroidota modulates membrane stability and host interactions

abstract: Modern western legal and criminal justice theories assume that punishment should deter criminalized behavior by introducing costs that reduce its expected utility, but, empirically, punishment often has weak effects on rates of crime and recidivism. Here, we hypothesize that when people are motivated to engage in criminalized behavior for moral reasons, they show diminished sensitivity to punishment. We demonstrate our hypothesis across 10 correlational, experimental, and economic game studies with participants drawn from the general population as well as participants with criminal backgrounds. Studies 1 to 3 draw on federal data of over 30,000 offenders and find that participants' estimates of moral motives for crime predict higher recidivism while estimates of material motives predict the opposite. Studies 4 to 8 use judgment studies and find that morally motivated crimes are less sensitive to punishment across a diversity of crime types, when motives are manipulated but actions are kept constant, persist for different types of consequences, and are unique to moral motivation. Studies 9 and 10 employ economic games and find that when players take money from others for moral reasons, they are less deterred by the imposition of fines. Implications for systems of punishment, offender psychology, and restorative justice approaches are discussed.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Morally motivated crimes are less sensitive to punishment

abstract: Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) poses a major public health threat without approved vaccines or antivirals. Its ribonucleoprotein (RNP) is essential for replication, but its native architecture and RNA packaging remain elusive. Here, we combine AI-based structural prediction with cryo-electron microscopy to resolve the native structure of the CCHFV RNP purified from CCHFV-infected cells. We report a 3.87 Å structure of a single-turn RNP, and local refinement yielded a 3.55 Å structure of two adjacent NP protomers with continuous RNA. This represents the highest-resolution authentic RNP structure reported among segmented negative-strand RNA viruses (sNSVs), and provides the structural basis for CCHFV RNP assembly. Together with mutational analyses, these findings define the molecular basis of RNA encapsidation and NP oligomerization in the native CCHFV RNP. Our findings provide a hybrid structural framework integrating AI and experimental approaches for understanding genome organization in sNSVs and offer a foundation for future antiviral development.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Authentic structure of the CCHFV RNA–nucleoprotein complex at near-atomic resolution

abstract: Can a model be identified from one experiment? We study analytic systems that are linearly parameterized by a combination of prescribed dictionary terms, such as partial differential operators and dynamical systems. For a single input-response pair, recovery is possible exactly when the evaluated dictionary terms are linearly independent. We prove a sharp zero-one law: either no input uniquely determines the coefficients, or almost every random input sampled from a nondegenerate Gaussian measure does. This dichotomy reduces one-shot system identification to a question about degenerate inputs and provides an a posteriori certificate in the noiseless setting. Numerical examples recover dynamical systems, nonlinear partial differential equations, and structured matrix families from single trajectory data, while also detecting when an extra probe is necessary.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: A zero-one law for one-shot system identification

abstract: Hydrophobic pores are generally expected to exclude ions because the large desolvation penalty associated with ion transfer cannot be compensated within a nonpolar environment. The envelope (E) protein of Middle East Respiratory Syndrome coronavirus (MERS-CoV) presents a striking exception, conducting cations with high efficiency despite forming a predominantly hydrophobic pore. To resolve this apparent paradox, we combine finite-temperature string simulations with additive and polarizable force fields to determine the minimum free-energy pathways for ion permeation through the MERS E channel. The simulations reveal a cooperative permeation mechanism in which transient counterion association, localized pore hydration, and electronic polarization jointly reduce the desolvation penalty. Rather than acting as passive spectators, counterions transiently chaperone the permeating cation before dissociating within the channel, thereby lowering the energetic cost of charge desolvation while preserving net ionic conductance. Explicit electronic polarization further reshapes the pore hydration landscape and cation-[Formula: see text] interactions, leading to substantially reduced free-energy barriers and a permeation mechanism that is in substantially better agreement with experiment. These results suggest that efficient ion transport through hydrophobic pores arises from the cooperative interplay between electrostatics, polarization, and hydration rather than complete pore wetting, providing both a mechanistic framework for MERS E protein function and a general physical principle for ion transport through biological and synthetic hydrophobic nanopores.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Counterions, polarization, and pore hydration relay drive ion permeation through hydrophobic pore formed by the MERS coronavirus E protein

abstract: Accumulation of senescent cells is increasingly viewed as a significant contributor to aging and age-related diseases. To date, the elimination of senescent cells through small molecule senolytic agents has largely relied on a limited number of repurposed agents, often leveraged from previous oncological applications. Here, we describe a CRISPR-based, genome-wide, synthetic lethal screen for senescent cells. From this screen, we identify a number of genes whose deletion appears to be well tolerated in normal proliferating cells, but whose deletion is lethal in the context of senescence. We further characterize one promising candidate gene encoding the ER-resident protein PARP16. Knockdown of PARP16 does not affect the viability of mouse or human cells but results in the death of a wide range of senescent cells. Furthermore, two distinct small molecule PARP16 inhibitors have little effect of normal cell growth but result in the selective death of senescent cells in culture and in freshly isolated human donor lung tissue explants. Together, these results demonstrate a rational strategy to identify novel senolytic therapies that could have potential applications for a wide range of age-related conditions.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: A genome-wide senescence synthetic lethality screen identifies PARP16 as a senolytic target

abstract: Substantial evidence shows that hypoxia-inducible factor 1α (HIF1α) up-regulates glycolytic enzymes and promotes lactate production, which contributes to “Warburg Effect.” Nevertheless, the impact of lactate or lactylation modification on hypoxia signaling pathways within the tumor microenvironment remains largely unclear. Here, we report that lactate can induce the upregulation of hypoxia pathway activity in a HIF1α-dependent manner. We identified that KAT5 as a lysine lactyltransferase of HIF1α and the “writer” responsible for lactylation at HIF1α K389, K460, K674, and K682, and HDAC2 as a HIF1α de-lactylase. The lactylation-deficient mutant of HIF1α (HIF1α 4KR ) reduced HIF1α stability, along with down-regulating hypoxia-mediated angiogenesis, metastasis, apoptosis, and glycolysis. Mechanistically, the HIF1α 4KR mutant enhances the binding of HIF1α to von Hippel-Lindau tumor suppressor protein (VHL), facilitating its degradation. MG149, a KAT5 inhibitor, can enhance the efficacy of anti-programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1)-based combination immunotherapy in a murine model by suppressing hypoxia pathway activity in tumor cells and potentiating the cytotoxic function of CD8 + T cells. Clinically, lactylated HIF1α and KAT5 are up-regulated in breast cancer tissues compared with adjacent tissues. Notably, elevated levels of HIF1α lactylation and KAT5 expression were observed in resistant cancer specimens from triple-negative breast cancer patients who had undergone neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy. Our results indicate that the tumor lactate microenvironment promotes the formation of the tumor hypoxic microenvironment by hijacking and lactylating HIF1α, and the KAT5–HIF1α Kla axis presents a promising therapeutic target for hypoxic tumors.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Lactate-rich tumor employs the KAT5–HIF1α axis to modulate the activity of the hypoxia pathway and facilitates tumor progression

abstract: To assess the ability of current AI systems to correctly solve research-level mathematics problems, we tested four AI systems on a set of ten problems in a broad range of mathematical fields; these problems arose naturally in the research process of the contributors. This document includes our methodology, and the results of our testing, including the assessment of human reviewers and a report of costs. We provide links to supplementary documents including the human solutions, the AI-generated solutions, and the referee reports and logs for the AI-generated solutions.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Harness design matters for AI capabilities in mathematics

abstract: We report the first integrated experiments of the double-cone ignition scheme, conducted on the ShenGuang II Upgrade facility using 14 kJ nanosecond laser beams and a 450 J picosecond (ps) laser beam. Two carbon-deuterium shells were imploded by the nanosecond laser beams inside dual compressing cones. Heated by the ps laser beam to $600\ifmmode\pm\else\textpm\fi{}50\text{ }\text{ }\mathrm{eV}$, we achieved a heating efficiency of $15.6\ifmmode\pm\else\textpm\fi{}6.2%$ and a consistent neutron yield of up to $(6.0\ifmmode\pm\else\textpm\fi{}0.5)\ifmmode\times\else\texttimes\fi{}{10}^{5}$, with a shot-to-shot fluctuation of only 7% across all three shots at optimal ps-laser timing delay. Multiscale simulations reveal that this high ps-laser-to-fuel heating efficiency originates from an extremely sharp compressed plasma density gradient with a simulated scale length of $\ensuremath{\sim}8\text{ }\text{ }\mathrm{\ensuremath{\mu}}\mathrm{m}$ at the edge of the high-density plateau, a unique geometric benefit of the double-cone architecture. The steep edge along the heating direction enables the heating cone to be placed as close as $35\text{ }\text{ }\mathrm{\ensuremath{\mu}}\mathrm{m}$ to the plasma center while preserving its structural integrity throughout ps-laser heating. This minimized separation mitigates energy losses caused by large divergence of relativistic electron beam generated by the ps-laser beam. We predict that heating efficiency can be further elevated to 20%--30% by scaling the laser energies to the levels of our next-generation high-energy laser facilities currently under construction.
title: High-Heating Efficiency and Reproducibility in Double-Cone Ignition Experiments

abstract: We analyze the two-dimensional Palatini Gauss-Bonnet theory on an infinite strip (product of a finite interval with the infinite line, corresponding to “time”). The theory has only boundary degrees of freedom. Its phase space is the cotangent bundle to the group manifold of S L ( 2 , R ) , subject to a (first-class) constraint quadratic in the momenta. With the simplest choice of boundary Hamiltonian, namely H = 0 , the theory is shown to describe geodesics on the group manifold of S L ( 2 , R ) , with a “mass” determined by the Palatini Gauss-Bonnet coupling constant. Other choices of boundary Hamiltonians compatible with gauge invariance are also possible. The symmetry group contains (left and right) group translations on S L ( 2 , R ) . These are “boundary symmetries” from the bulk point of view, with one copy acting on one end of the interval and the other copy acting on the other end. Comments on the quantum theory are also given.
title: Exact Solution of Two-Dimensional Palatini Gauss-Bonnet Theory on a Strip

abstract: We report neutron powder diffraction measurements and path-integral molecular dynamics simulations of stacking-disorder-free cubic ice I c , produced by topotactic degassing of C2 hydrogen hydrate. Across the cryogenic stability range, ice I c exhibits a density maximum near 70 K, closely matching that of hexagonal ice I h despite their different long-range stacking sequences. Negative thermal expansion in ice I is therefore not specific to hexagonal stacking, but arises from the shared open tetrahedral hydrogen-bond network. Simulations with the MB-pol potential quantitatively reproduce the experimental anomaly only when nuclear quantum effects are included. The density maximum coincides, within the temperature resolution, with maximal anisotropy of the proton quantum distribution. Neutron-derived displacement parameters independently reveal a strongly enhanced transverse proton displacement, while phonon calculations identify low-frequency transverse modes with the most negative Grüneisen parameters. Together, these results establish the negative thermal expansion of ice I as a collective quantum effect governed by nuclear statistics and the dynamics of the hydrogen-bond network.
title: Negative thermal expansion in cubic ice: A collective quantum effect of the hydrogen-bond network

abstract: We calculate the dimension-six Δ Q = 0 four-quark matrix elements describing heavy-meson lifetime ratios using the gradient flow with its short flow-time expansion (SFTX) as a renormalization procedure. On six RBC/UKQCD 2 + 1 -flavor domain-wall fermion ensembles, we determine flowed bag parameters for physical charm and strange quarks and match to the MS ¯ scheme with perturbative SFTX coefficients through next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO). A multiscale matching procedure using renormalization-group running improves the extrapolation to zero flow time. For the operators relevant to τ ( D s ) / τ ( D 0 ) at the SU ( 3 ) F symmetric point, we obtain B 1 MS ¯ ( 3 GeV ) = 1.0524 ( 97 ) , B 2 MS ¯ ( 3 GeV ) = 0.9621 ( 70 ) , ε 1 MS ¯ ( 3 GeV ) = − 0.2275 ( 76 ) , and ε 2 MS ¯ ( 3 GeV ) = − 0.0005 ( 8 ) using a specific choice of evanescent operators. This is the first lattice-QCD determination of Δ Q = 0 four-quark operators with a full error budget. It opens the path toward higher-precision predictions of heavy-meson lifetimes and similar quantities exhibiting operator mixing under renormalization.
title: Bag Parameters for Heavy Meson Lifetimes from a Lattice QCD Calculation at the SU ( 3 ) F -symmetric Point

abstract: We search for the pionic transitions χ c 1 ( 3872 ) → π 0 χ c J ( 1 P ) ( J = 0 , 1 , 2 ) and χ c 0 ( 3915 ) → π 0 χ c 1 in B + → π 0 χ c J K + decays using the Belle and Belle~II data samples collected at the Υ ( 4 S ) resonance, corresponding to integrated luminosities of 711 f b − 1 and 492 f b − 1 , respectively. We report the first evidence for the decay χ c 1 ( 3872 ) → π 0 χ c 0 with a significance of 3.4 σ , including systematic uncertainties. We measure the product of branching fractions ${\cal B}(B^+\to \chi_{c1}(3872)K^+)\times{\cal B}(\chi_{c1}(3872)\to\pi^0\chi_{c0})=(20.0\pm6.8\pm2.3)\times10^{-6}$ and the branching fraction ratio ${\cal B}(\chi_{c1}(3872)\to\pi^0\chi_{c0})/{\cal B}(\chi_{c1}(3872)\to\pi^+\pi^-J/\psi)=2.3\pm0.8\pm0.4$ , where the first and second uncertainties are statistical and systematic, respectively. The upper limits at 90% credibility on the products of branching fractions for the π 0 χ c 1 and π 0 χ c 2 modes are 7.5 × 10 − 6 and 15.3 × 10 − 6 , respectively. The corresponding upper limits on the branching fraction ratios relative to the π + π − J / ψ decay are 0.9 and 1.8 . The measured branching fractions for χ c 1 ( 3872 ) → π 0 χ c J are consistent with several theoretical predictions based on the hadronic molecular interpretation of the χ c 1 ( 3872 ) . No significant signal is seen for the χ c 0 ( 3915 ) → π 0 χ c 1 decay, and we set the 90% credibility upper limit of ${\cal B}(B^+\to \chi_{c0}(3915)K^+)\times{\cal B}(\chi_{c0}(3915)\to\pi^0\chi_{c1})<6.6\times10^{-6}$ , while the decays for J = 0 and 2 are forbidden by parity conservation.
title: First evidence of χ c 1 ( 3872 ) → π 0 χ c 0 ( 1 P ) and search for χ c 0 ( 3915 ) → π 0 χ c 1 ( 1 P )

abstract: Spontaneous breaking of time-translation symmetry and the emergence of self-sustained oscillations in quantum driven-dissipative systems are the hallmark of continuous time crystals (CTCs). An outstanding challenge is to achieve precise, coherent control of such dynamical phases, whose complex nonlinear dynamics makes them inherently difficult to manipulate. Here, we experimentally demonstrate coherent control of a solid-state CTC realized in a non-resonantly excited spin-polarized exciton-polariton condensate in a Ga(Al)As microcavity. By tuning a weak control laser energy and power, we stabilize distinct dynamical regimes, including frequency pushing, injection locking with continuous tuning of the limit-cycle frequency, and full suppression of the autonomous dynamics via phase locking. Under appropriate detuning conditions, the control excitation generates coherent mechanical self-oscillation through the polariton–phonon deformation-potential interaction, evidenced by spectral sidebands. The resulting dynamical back-action provides a phonon-mediated locking channel that fixes the frequency of the CTC. Together, the two channels dramatically enhance the temporal coherence of the GHz limit-cycle dynamics, as established through linewidth narrowing and time-resolved first-order correlation measurements $\gone(\tau)$ . Our work establishes a way to harness the unique aspects of CTCs for practical applications in the GHz-range.
title: Coherent control of a polariton continuous time crystal

abstract: Speeding up the relaxation dynamics of many-body quantum systems is important in a variety of contexts, including quantum computation and state preparation. We demonstrate that such acceleration can be universally achieved via transient stochastic resetting. This means that during an initial time interval of finite duration, the dynamics is interrupted by resets that take the system to a designated state at randomly selected times. We illustrate this idea for few-body open systems and also for a challenging many-body case, where a first-order phase transition leads to a divergence of relaxation time. In all scenarios, a significant and sometimes even exponential acceleration in reaching the stationary state is observed, similar to the so-called Mpemba effect. The universal nature of this speedup lies in the fact that the design of the resetting protocol only requires knowledge of a few macroscopic properties of the target state, such as the order parameter of the phase transition, while it does not necessitate any fine-tuned manipulation of the initial state.
title: Universal Relaxation Speedup in Nonequilibrium Quantum Many-Body Systems through Transient Resetting

abstract: We study nonstabilizerness on the information lattice and demonstrate that noninteger local information directly indicates nonstabilizerness. For states with a clear separation of short- and large-scale information, a noninteger total information at large scales Γ serves as a witness of long-range nonstabilizerness. We propose a folding procedure to separate the global and edge-to-edge contributions to Γ . As an example we show that the ferromagnetic ground state of the spin- 1 / 2 three-state Potts model has long-range nonstabilizerness originating from global correlations, while the paramagnetic ground state has at most short-range nonstabilizerness.
title: Witnessing Short- and Long-Range Nonstabilizerness via the Information Lattice

abstract: In wire-array Z pinches, plasma ablation shapes the conditions for the subsequent implosion. Resolving separate ion and electron motion in these dense, magnetized flows remains an experimental challenge. Here, we report the first direct, spatially resolved measurements of radial (${J}_{r}$) and azimuthal (${J}_{\ensuremath{\theta}}$) current densities in Z-pinch ablation, enabled by a Bayesian inversion framework unifying two-angle Thomson scattering, interferometry, and Faraday rotation. We infer an inward ambipolar radial electric field, ${E}_{r}\ensuremath{\approx}\ensuremath{-}3.3\ifmmode\times\else\texttimes\fi{}{10}^{4}\text{ }\text{ }\mathrm{V}/\mathrm{m}$, that accelerates ions; the azimuthal current is attributed to the Hall effect. This two-fluid mechanism offers a possible common explanation for two long-standing macroscopic signatures: an anode-directed ablation-flow tilt of $(8.2\ifmmode\pm\else\textpm\fi{}2.9)\ifmmode^\circ\else\textdegree\fi{}$, attributed to $\mathbf{E}\ifmmode\times\else\texttimes\fi{}\mathbf{B}$ drift, and a cathode-to-anode asymmetry of approximately $14\text{ }\text{ }\mathrm{T}$ in the path-averaged parallel field ($⟨{B}_{\ensuremath{\parallel}}⟩\ensuremath{\approx}{B}_{\ensuremath{\theta}}$). The magnetic asymmetry may contribute to seeding the zipper effect. A hybrid particle-in-cell simulation in axisymmetric $(r,z)$ geometry provides supporting evidence that ${J}_{r}$, ${E}_{r}$, and an anode-directed drift can arise in ablation flows, though its reduced geometry limits quantitative comparison with the two-wire experiment.
title: Two-Fluid Effects in Z-Pinch Ablation Characterized by Unified Bayesian Inversion

abstract: We study the conditions under which matrix product states (MPSs) or matrix product operators are exact eigenvectors of an extensive local operator such as a Hamiltonian. By suitably choosing the local operator, this covers a wide range of settings: exact eigenstates of Hamiltonians, including scar states; exact MPS trajectories for driven quantum systems; steady states of local Lindbladians; generalized symmetries of either Hamiltonians or density matrices; and many more. Our key result is that a local, fixed-size equation—namely, how a single term in the operator acts on a block of tensors—provides a necessary and sufficient condition for exact solutions. This local characterization allows us to obtain the full space of MPS solutions to all of the aforementioned problems; in particular, we exemplify the power of our results by recovering the quantum group symmetries of the XXZ model. We also discuss applications to numerical algorithms with MPSs and the generalization of our results to 2D, i.e., projected entangled pair states.
title: Local Characterization of Global Tensor Network Eigenstates

abstract: Charged kaon-deuteron interactions offer a sensitive probe of the strangeness sector of QCD at low energy, particularly through their scattering parameters. Despite available theoretical predictions, experimental constraints remain absent, particularly for the K − d system. The first measurement of femtoscopic correlation functions for K − d ⊕ K + d ¯ and K + d ⊕ K − d ¯ particle pairs in Pb-Pb collisions at s NN = 5.02 TeV recorded by ALICE at the LHC is presented. Correlation functions for both systems are analyzed in three centrality classes and fitted using the Lednický-Lyuboshitz model to extract the source size and strong interaction scattering lengths. The K − d scattering length is found to be ℜ f 0 = − 1.44 ± 0.15 ( stat ) − 0.10 + 0.10 ( stat ) fm and ℑ f 0 = 1.34 ± 0.33 ( stat ) − 0.15 + 0.21 ( syst ) fm , while for K + d the value ℜ f 0 = − 0.68 ± 0.16 ( stat ) − 0.09 + 0.09
title: First Measurement of the Strong Interaction Scattering Parameters for the K − d and K + d Systems

abstract: Standard continuous gravitational-wave searches with pulsar timing arrays (PTAs) neglect cosmological redshift, restricting their applicability to the local Universe. We introduce a redshift-aware PTA framework and apply it to the Parkes PTA Data Release 3, deriving the first direct constraints on supermassive binary black holes (SMBBHs) at the cosmic dawn. Evaluating our limits across a broad redshift range, we observationally establish the non-monotonic mass-redshift exclusion boundary driven by the theoretical ``redshift bias", demonstrating how PTAs can effectively probe sources at extreme distances. Redshift-aware targeted searches toward high-redshift systems, including the ultraluminous quasar J0100+2802 ($z=6.327$) and the JWST-discovered galaxy JADES-GS-z14-0 ($z=14.32$), rigorously exclude SMBBHs with chirp masses $\mathcal{M}_c \gtrsim 10^{10} M_\odot$ across the nanohertz frequency band. Finally, we demonstrate that high-redshift binaries can be robustly detected and localized, allowing for the accurate measurement of their intrinsic properties. Our results provide the tightest constraints to date on SMBBHs at $z > 6$ and establish a practical framework for probing early-Universe black hole assembly.
title: Nanohertz Gravitational-Wave Constraints on Supermassive Binary Black Holes at Cosmic Dawn

abstract: Electrides are unique materials in which electrons occupy interstitial regions formed by cation frameworks and act as anions. They have many interesting properties and are often induced by high pressure in some materials. Understanding the emergence of electride states is a central problem in condensed-matter physics. While existing theoretical frameworks, including the interstitial quasi-atom (ISQ) and electron-ion interaction (EII) models, have provided some useful phenomenological interpretations of the electride formation, the atomistic origin and the underlying physics of this charge redistribution remain unclear. Here, within a first-principles framework, we systematically study the evolution of electronic structures of compressed materials, using alkali metals as representative examples. By mapping symmetry-resolved electronic band states onto atomic orbitals, we find that (i) pressure-induced quantum confinement raises the energies of atomic orbitals due to enhanced kinetic energy and increased overlap between valence and core electrons, with the energy shift being larger for more delocalized s orbital than for more localized p and d orbitals; and (ii) this effect causes reordering of band states, making the electride states, which are composed of the interatomic hybridized pd orbitals, to progressively shift in energy below the s orbital states, leading to their occupation and the onset of electride behavior. This microscopic electronic-state picture clarifies the origin of the electride formation and provides a general framework for understanding the evolution of interstitial electronic states under compression across diverse materials.
title: Origin of Electride States and Their Responses under Pressure

abstract: Secondary-phase fillers usually strengthen metals at the expense of plasticity and functionality. Here, we show that embedding stimulus-responsive, shape-memory ceramics into a metal activates a transformation-induced plasticity response through a distinct constraint-relief mechanism. During processing, matrix constraint stabilizes metastable austenite in ceramics; during deformation, progressive local stress relief drives the free-energy change negative and triggers martensitic transformation inside the metal. As a proof of concept, aluminum (Al) containing 20 wt.% transformable zirconia exhibits a twofold increase in uniform elongation vis-\`a-vis Al with nontransformable zirconia, together with an ultimate tensile strength about 50% higher than monolithic Al. The transformation-induced lattice expansion promotes dislocation storage, sustains strain hardening, and suppresses crack initiation, thereby delaying strain localization. These results establish ceramic phase transformation in metals as a new route to plasticize, strengthen, and functionalize structural alloys.
title: Transformation-Induced Plasticity in Metals Activated by Shape-Memory Ceramics

abstract: The realization of scalable quantum networks for distribution of entanglement over long distances hinges on quantum repeaters. To outperform the exponential transmission loss in optical fibers, quantum repeaters must employ multiplexing schemes in the temporal, spectral, or spatial domain. The performance of such a multiplexed scheme is contingent on efficient quantum memories offering both extended storage times and large multimode capacities. Toward this goal, we experimentally demonstrate a memory platform operating at telecom wavelength using an ${\mathrm{Er}}^{3+}:{\mathrm{Y}}_{2}{\mathrm{SiO}}_{5}$ crystal. We record on-demand storage and recall of weak coherent pulses for up to 1 ms, exceeding by an order of magnitude that of previously reported demonstrations based on ${\mathrm{Er}}^{3+}$. The memory exhibits an efficiency of 10.36% at $300\text{ }\text{ }\mathrm{\ensuremath{\mu}}\mathrm{s}$ storage time with a signal-to-noise ratio of 10.9, mainly limited by spontaneous emission noise. We also store two spectral modes representing a frequency-bin encoding and retrieve the state with an overlap of 81.8%. Furthermore, we demonstrate multimode capacity by simultaneously storing 20 temporal and 3 spectral modes with on-demand and selective recall capabilities, serving as a promising step toward a scalable quantum repeater architecture.
title: On-Demand Millisecond Storage of Spectrotemporal Modes at Telecom Wavelength

abstract: We report the experimental observation of memory effects in a vertically vibrated thin granular layer. Following a quench in the input acceleration, the granular temperature exhibits an anomalous Kovacs memory effect confined to the initial fast relaxation stage. This memory vanishes shortly thereafter, yielding a time-dependent memoryless regime governed solely by the instantaneous temperature before the system reaches its final steady state. We develop a kinetic theory framework that quantitatively captures these features by identifying the initial memory and subsequent memoryless regimes with the kinetic and hydrodynamic states, respectively (that are well established in kinetic theory). Our analysis reveals that memory emerges during fast transients through coupling between horizontal and vertical temperatures, a mechanism that fundamentally constrains the accessible memory phenomenology and precludes observation of the standard Kovacs effect in this system. Molecular dynamics simulations provide independent confirmation of all experimental and theoretical findings.
title: Kovacs Memory Effect in a Thin Granular Layer: Experimental Evidence and Its Physical Origin

abstract: Contemporary understanding of thermalization in quantum field theory stems largely from understanding properties of transient excitations of equilibria. These nonhydrodynamic excitations are known to structurally differ between weakly and strongly coupled quantum field theories with no known results at intermediate values of the interaction strength. We demonstrate that all the known behaviors of transient excitations can be understood as a consequence of different realizations of a symmetry principle, the shift symmetry, applied at the level of the far-from-equilibrium generalization of the hydrodynamic effective action that we explicitly construct. Our approach naturally includes the effects of stochastic fluctuations outside the hydrodynamic regime and allows to explicitly construct hybrid models interpolating between weak- and strong-coupling behavior. We study properties of one such model motivated by thermalization in nuclear collisions in light of the QCD running coupling.
title: Building Far-from-Equilibrium Effective Field Theories Using Shift Symmetries

abstract: We theoretically propose a Hall effect driven by effective gravitational fields arising from quantum geometry. We identify four mechanisms for this ``emergent-gravity Hall effect'': real-space gravity, momentum-space gravity, gravitational anomalous velocity, and gravitational Lorentz force, all of which are described by Christoffel symbols in real, momentum, or time spaces. Based on the semiclassical theory, we construct a unified theoretical framework to systematically investigate how emergent gravity in these spaces affects transport phenomena. We demonstrate these effects through model calculations and clarify the conditions under which a finite Hall response can arise. Our findings open a new avenue for exploring gravitational effects in quantum systems.
title: Emergent-Gravity Hall Effect from Quantum Geometry

abstract: We find that heavy quark transport beyond leading logarithm at weak coupling is intrinsically non-Gaussian: the longitudinal momentum transfer distribution has that are crucial for equilibration dynamics. We show this by computing the leading-order momentum transfer kernel for relativistic heavy quarks in weakly coupled non-Abelian plasmas, matching perturbative momentum transfer on the thermal scale to hard-thermal-loop-resummed soft physics. This is the same structure previously found in strongly coupled holographic plasmas, showing that it is not peculiar to weak or strong coupling, conformality, or supersymmetry. We therefore expect that this is a robust feature that physical quark-gluon plasma should also exhibit.
title: Heavy Quark Transport Is Non-Gaussian beyond Leading Logarithm

abstract: Experimental and theoretical studies of the high-pressure phases of hydrogen are highly sensitive to methodological choices. We compare the cold phase diagram of hydrogen calculated between 400-700 GPa with meta-GGA functionals (R2SCAN and SCAN0) with the commonly employed GGA-PBE functional. Molecular phases are stabilized over atomic phase to higher pressures with the meta-GGA, in closer agreement with diffusion Monte Carlo calculations. R2SCAN phonon spectra show that the dynamical instabilities and anharmonic signatures predicted at the GGA level vanish, indicating that such effects may partly arise from functional deficiencies rather than quantum nuclear effects. Bonding analysis reveals that PBE artificially weakens intramolecular H–H bonds and enhances intermolecular interactions through charge delocalization, whereas meta-GGA preserves a more localized molecular character.
title: Quantum effects or theoretical artifacts? A computational reanalysis of hydrogen’s high-pressure phase stability and properties

abstract: Quantum gases are used to simulate the physics of the lowest Landau level with neutral atoms, which in the simplest setup is achieved by rotating the gas at the confining harmonic trap frequency, a requirement that is difficult to meet in practice. However, it is known that lowest Landau level states appear among the excited states of weakly interacting gases, even in a nonrotating trap, by working at fixed finite angular momentum. Thus, even in the absence of rotations or for moderate rotation frequencies, fractional quantum Hall (FQH) states can be accessed as excited states at finite angular momentum. Motivated by this, and by recent experimentally demonstrated excitation protocols for two particles, we show that such states can be selectively addressed at larger particle numbers, and we propose imaging techniques to resolve their distinct microscopic structure. In particular, we suggest that recently developed excitation and imaging techniques for rotating few-fermion systems allow for a detailed experimental investigation of FQH wave functions and of the crossover to large particle numbers. We illustrate the evolution of the excitation spectrum with rotations at weak interactions for N = 6 spin-balanced fermions and show how sampling of the few-body wave function allows one to discriminate between total guiding-center, center-of-mass vortex, and hyperradial excitations, thus providing detailed and versatile probes of the microscopic structure of FQH states.
title: Probing Fractional Quantum Hall States in Weakly Interacting Fermi Gases

abstract: Bright squeezing in multiple discrete frequency modes is important to implement quantum-enhanced spectroscopy and optical quantum computing applications. Here, we propose a way to achieve topologically protected squeezing through the down-conversion process in the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model along synthetic frequency dimension. The edge states localize the squeezing at the frequency boundary modes, protecting the squeezed light from the perturbations and supporting tunable squeezed modes. Moreover, our model can lead to broadband bright squeezed frequency comb, inducing the multipartite entanglement between the comb line modes with the robustness. Our proposal suggests the generation of a topologically protected multimode bright squeezing, which gives an important platform for exploring topological multipartite entanglement for robust cluster-state generation.
title: Multimode Squeezing and Multipartite Entanglement Generations with Topological Protection

abstract: Encircling exceptional points (EPs) in non-Hermitian systems has been shown to induce chiral state transfer, whereby the final state of the system is always the lowest-loss eigenstate, independent of the input. When multiple lowest-loss states coexist, it is generally expected that EP encirclement yields mixed outputs composed of these states. Here we reveal a distinct regime, peculiar of non-Hermitian systems hosting multiple iso-imaginary Riemann surfaces, extending the conventional understanding of EP dynamics. We find that states residing on higher-loss Riemann surfaces preferentially undergo nonadiabatic transitions to the nearest lower-loss surface, while transitions between iso imaginary surfaces are strongly suppressed. This fixed-selection-rule dynamics enables input-state-dependent chiral transfer, such that encircling the same EP produces distinct and well-defined output states for different inputs, rather than mixed output states. We experimentally demonstrate this mechanism in a photonic platform, revealing new EP dynamics beyond conventional chiral state transfer, and opening a pathway towards mode-selective, high-capacity non-Hermitian photonic devices.
title: Input-State-Dependent Chiral State Transfer Enabled by Iso-Imaginary Riemann Surfaces

abstract: Walk-on-Spheres (WoS) is a particle-based technique used to describe physical phenomena as diverse as electrostatics, heat conduction, rendering, ion transport, and chemical reactions. It is fast, scalable, meshless, and applicable to geometrically complex domains, as long as the governing equations have constant coefficients. Despite these advantages, WoS has persistently struggled to deal with spatial heterogeneity, exhibiting significant loss of either accuracy or efficiency. We introduce a WoS method for parabolic and elliptic problems with spatially varying coefficients and demonstrate its superior performance through applications to heterogeneous transport phenomena. The method exhibits small bias and, where transport heterogeneity dominates the overall dynamics, a variance per sample is 1 to 2 orders of magnitude smaller than that of competing methods, including state-of-the-art WoS algorithms.
title: Walk-on-Spheres Solution to Heterogeneous Transport Phenomena

abstract: We study the superradiant phase transition of a mesoscopic Fermi gas comprising between a few tens and a few thousand $^{6}\mathrm{Li}$ atoms in a high-finesse cavity across a wide range of densities. We observe a nonmonotonic variation of the superradiant threshold as a function of density, with a minimum reached when the Fermi and recoil wave vectors are comparable. The minimum corresponds to a crossover between Fermi pressure-assisted ordering and Pauli blocking of photon scattering, in good agreement with theory. This interpretation is confirmed by a study of the atom-number dependence of the ordering threshold and photon number scaling. Our system opens the perspective of studying few-fermion systems with strong and coherent light-matter coupling.
title: Fermi-Pressure-Assisted Superradiant Transition with a Mesoscopic Fermi Gas in a Cavity

abstract: The recently developed conditional probability density functional theory (CP DFT) yields direct access to the exchange-correlation hole of a system, an important correlation function that is not available in standard DFT. We present the first results for extended materials with periodic boundary conditions. We validate CP DFT for weakly correlated Na and Si. We apply it to a stretched hydrogen chain, the prototype of strong correlation. When applied to the kagome material ${\mathrm{CsV}}_{3}{\mathrm{Sb}}_{5}$, we find $d$-orbital correlations that are missing in standard DFT, implying an enhanced finding probability between two separated electrons and a local charge density wave related modulation.
title: Conditional Probability Density Functional Theory for Solids

abstract: Hilbert space fragmentation refers to exponential growth in the number of dynamically disconnected Krylov sectors with system size. It is taken as evidence of ergodicity breaking, since conventional symmetries generate at most a polynomial number of sectors. However, we demonstrate that generalized symmetries, including higher-form, subsystem, and gauge symmetries, can have exponentially many symmetry sectors in the tensor product basis. We further prove that noninvertible symmetries can induce additional fragmentation within individual symmetry sectors. Fragmentation in several known models arises from generalized symmetries, and the presence of exponentially many Krylov sectors therefore does not by itself imply ergodicity breaking. Finally, we show that disorder free localization arises from Krylov-restricted thermalization when sectors lack translation invariance, requiring neither ergodicity breaking nor gauge symmetry.
title: Hilbert Space Fragmentation from Generalized Symmetries

abstract: We simulate nanoscale ice-glass friction from first principles and upscale it by modeling frictional heating. Nanoscale simulations alone overestimate friction and miss its velocity dependence. Frictional heating warms the contact toward the melting point, thickening the premelting film tenfold and cutting its viscosity a hundredfold; friction drops with velocity, matching experiment. Premelting forms the film without sliding or heating, but its slipperiness hinges on frictional heating, as Bowden and Hughes proposed in 1939, without melting. Snow, other materials, and coatings remain open.
title: Why Ice Is So Slippery

abstract: We present the first study of short-baseline neutrino oscillation searches using a tagged neutrino beamline, taking the proposed nuSCOPE facility at CERN as a benchmark. In this Letter we demonstrate that tagged neutrino beams, where the neutrino flavor, energy, and propagation distance are determined with exceptional event-by-event precision, provide a new experimental approach to search for non-standard neutrino oscillations. We evaluate the sensitivity to sterile-neutrino-induced oscillations in the ν μ disappearance, ν μ → ν e appearance, and ν e disappearance channels, demonstrating the ability to probe multiple flavor transitions and both appearance and disappearance modes within a single experiment. Our results show that tagged beams enable sensitivity improvements to mass-squared splittings spanning several orders of magnitude while substantially reducing the dependence on neutrino flux predictions that limits conventional searches. We find that nuSCOPE can probe a broad region of parameter space motivated by existing anomalies and extend coverage into previously unexplored territory, demonstrating the strong potential of tagged neutrino beams for precision oscillation physics.
title: Novel approach to short baseline oscillation searches using neutrino tagging with nuSCOPE

abstract: We propose a protocol to adiabatically prepare a many-particle fractional quantum Hall fluid of bosonic ultracold atoms exploiting a time-dependent coherent coupling of a strongly interacting atomic state with a large dilute Bose-Einstein condensate.
