Starting from an empty cloud, atoms with well-defined angular momentum are coherently pumped into the fluid by Raman beams with a Laguerre-Gauss profile. Compared to number-conserving schemes which rely on finite-size-induced gaps, we identify an adiabatic path in the Fock space which avoids crossing fixed-particle-number phase transitions and maintains a sizable and externally controlled adiabatic gap open at all times. The efficiency of our preparation protocol is numerically assessed for typical experimental parameters up to particle numbers that largely exceed the experimental state of the art. The crucial advantage of including an anharmonic confinement is finally highlighted.
title: Adiabatic Preparation of a Fractional Quantum Hall Fluid by Coherently Pumping Atoms from a Bose-Einstein Condensate

abstract: First-principles descriptions of correlated quantum materials require a simultaneous treatment of strong local many-body effects and nonlocal dynamical screening. We present an efficient fully self-consistent implementation of G W +EDMFT that combines nonlocal correlations at the G W level with a non-perturbative treatment of local correlations within extended dynamical mean-field theory (EDMFT), with a well-defined double-counting correction and a self-consistently determined impurity interaction. Self-consistency in both the Green’s function and the dynamically screened interaction is essential for describing screening processes across energy scales. A key ingredient that makes it computationally feasible is the compression of two-particle correlation functions using interpolative separable density fitting (ISDF). Applying the scheme to the Mott insulator SrMnO 3 and the correlated metal LaNiO 3 , we show that the self-consistent effective local interaction resolves the overscreening inherent to constrained-RPA approaches. For SrMnO 3 , this stabilizes a Mott-insulating state in quantitative agreement with experiment, while for LaNiO 3 local EDMFT corrections yield a quasiparticle mass enhancement consistent with ARPES. These results establish fully self-consistent G W +EDMFT as a reliable framework for strongly correlated quantum materials.
title: Electronic correlations and dynamical screening with ab initio quantum embedding

abstract: In solids, frequent electron-electron collisions can induce collective, fluid-like electron transport. While this regime offers a powerful framework for exploring many-body phenomena, there is still a lack in functional electronic device actively exploiting hydrodynamic behaviour of electrons. Here, we introduce a solid-state analogue of a Tesla valve — a passive fluidic diode that rectifies flow without moving parts. Lithographically defined in high-mobility GaAs two-dimensional electron gas, the device exhibits abrupt rectification producing a more than tenfold difference between forward and reverse resistances. This threshold behaviour, reminiscent of the onset of turbulence in fluidic Tesla valves, points to the emergence of turbulent regime in the electron liquid — a long-predicted, but yet unobserved state of electronic matter. More broadly, our work demonstrates the fruitfulness of the hydrodynamic analogy: fluidic technologies can be readily adopted to create novel electronic devices. Here, this is realized through a solid-state rectifier whose operation relies on a new physical mechanism, interparticle collisions.
title: Rectification at High Currents in Asymmetric Two-Dimensional Electron Structures: Electron Tesla Valve

abstract: We report ultrafast dissociation of gas-phase water following photoexcitation above the O 1s ionization threshold. High-resolution resonant Auger spectroscopy reveals sharp constant-kinetic-energy features arising from nonradiative decay of neutral atomic oxygen formed within the O 1s core-hole lifetime. Comparison with Auger spectra identifies these features as transitions from the atomic ( 1 s ) 1 ( 2 s ) 2 ( 2 p ) 5 1 P state, demonstrating that neutral fragments can form in well-defined electronic states before Auger decay.
title: Ultrafast Dissociation of Water Producing Atomic Oxygen following Excitation above the O 1s Threshold

abstract: Magic and entanglement are independent quantum resources, yet their exact relation in many-body dynamics has remained elusive. We uncover two structural principles. First, at any stabilizer state, the curvature of the second stabilizer R'enyi entropy under an arbitrary Hermitian generator equals the quantum Fisher information up to a fixed normalization, creating a bidirectional bridge between computational and metrological resources. Second, for commuting Ising evolution on any forest graph, a Clifford pruning circuit yields the full stabilizer-R'enyi family at arbitrary size and in any spatial embedding, thereby furnishing a graph-theoretic construction of families with finite magic density and vanishing entanglement density in the thermodynamic limit. We solve two paradigmatic one-dimensional realizations central to quantum simulation—an Ising quench and a kicked Floquet chain—exactly for arbitrary system size and directly in the thermodynamic limit, revealing finite magic density with vanishing entanglement density, distinct magic and entanglement revival periods, and Clifford points with zero magic but finite bipartite entanglement. The same tangent geometry fixes initial growth and perturbative revival lifting, and a replica cluster expansion establishes the stability of thermodynamic magic minima uniformly in system size. Large scale Pauli-basis matrix-product-state calculations verify all predictions, and the tangent bridge yields a concrete protocol for detecting magic near stabilizer reference states through established quantum-Fisher-information measurements.
title: Magic without entanglement: Exact revivals and their Fisher information origin

abstract: A first observation of the rare decay η → μ + μ − e + e − is reported by the CMS Collaboration at the CERN LHC. The result is based on a proton-proton collision data sample at s = 13.6 TeV corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 38.0 fb − 1 , acquired in 2022 using a high-rate dimuon trigger. Using the η → μ + μ − γ decay channel for normalization, the branching fraction is measured to be B ( η → μ + μ − e + e − ) = ( 2.4 ± 0.8 ) × 10 − 6 , with the uncertainty including statistical and systematic sources as well as the B ( η → μ + μ − γ ) uncertainty. This result is about a factor of 3 smaller than the existing limit and is consistent with recent theoretical predictions.
title: Observation of the Rare Decay η → μ + μ − e + e −

abstract: Noncontacting light control of ferroelectric (FE) order has been receiving extensive interest in condensed matter physics. In this work, we investigate near-resonant light irradiation that induces structure-dependent photoexcited carrier density along the transition pathway. We combine a minimal Rice-Mele model containing intersite density-density correlations with ab initio calculations for realistic materials such as GeTe and SnTe. If the photon energy is below-gap without carrier excitation, only off-resonant scattering occurs and the FE order tends to be diminished. Slightly increasing photon energy at the near-gap regime would lead to a centrosymmetric non-polar (NP) to FE phase transition, which is not thermally accessible in conventional pressure-temperature phase diagram. This is in contrast to the well-above-gap light situation that tends to suppress the FE order under a fixed amount of photoexcitation. We apply phenomenological Landau theory and show that they belong to the continuous and first-order phase transitions, respectively. The occupation constrained calculations suggest that these reversible NP-FE phase transitions could be triggered under moderate light fluence. Our mechanism provides a potential route to reversible light-stabilized polar phases with reduced lattice heating and marginal lattice damages.
title: Manipulation of ferroelectric polarization under near-gap light

abstract: Combining magnetometry with optical spectroscopy has uncovered novel quantum phenomena and is emerging as a powerful probe of quantum materials. However, the theory of the magnetic response of excitons, correlated electron-hole pairs in insulators, remains incomplete due to insufficient treatment of electron-hole interactions and quantum geometric effects. In biased bilayer graphene, for instance, theoretical predictions of valley $g$ factors for $p$ excitons deviate from experiment by nearly an order of magnitude. Here, we develop a quantum theory of the exciton orbital magnetic moment, based on first-order perturbation theory within the GW plus Bethe-Salpeter equation approach and a rigorous treatment of the position operator in the response of exciton states to a magnetic field. Our formalism reveals three distinct contributions that go beyond the heuristic approaches used in the literature: a Berry-phase-corrected single-particle electron and hole moment difference, a term from envelope-function winding linked to electron-hole relative motion, and a center-of-mass correction from exciton band quantum geometry, with the latter two being completely new effects not considered in previous studies. Our ab initio calculations yield results in excellent agreement with experiment, establishing the importance of interaction and quantum geometric effects in the magnetic response of excitons.
title: Quantum Theory of Exciton Magnetic Moment: Interaction and Quantum Geometric Effects

abstract: The tunable interaction between stationary quantum bits and propagating modes of light allows for the encoding of quantum information in the state of itinerant photons. This ability fulfills a central requirement for quantum networking, enabling quantum state transfer between distant quantum devices. Conventionally, a symmetric envelope of the photon wave packet is used for such purposes. Yet, the use of alternative temporal modes enables multiple applications in waveguide quantum electrodynamics that remain unexplored experimentally. Here, we use superconducting quantum circuits to generate individual itinerant microwave photons shaped in three mutually orthogonal temporal modes. We transfer the created photons across a 30-m cryogenic link, showing that the orthogonality allows us to decide at the receiver which mode to absorb, reflecting the other two with a selectivity ratio of 40. This experimental capability extends the microwave-frequency quantum communication toolbox, enabling a new photonic degree of freedom.
title: Emission and Absorption of Microwave Photons in Orthogonal Temporal Modes across a 30-Meter Two-Node Network

abstract: We investigate superconducting transmission lines as a novel platform for realizing a quantum fluid of microwave photons in a propagating geometry. We anticipate that the strong photon-photon interactions provided by the intrinsic nonlinearity of Josephson junctions are sufficient to enter a regime of strongly interacting photons for realistic parameters. To prove the potential of this platform, we show that a suitable tapering of the transmission line parameters allows for the adiabatic conversion of an incident coherent field into a cold Tonks-Girardeau gas of fermionized photons close to its ground state. Signatures of the strong correlations are visible in the correlation properties of the transmitted light.
title: From Coherent to Fermionized Microwave Photons in a Superconducting Transmission Line

abstract: We spectroscopically study mobile impurities immersed in a homogeneous bosonic bath (a box-trapped Bose gas), varying the bath temperature and the strength of impurity-bath interactions. We compare our results to those for a quasipure Bose-Einstein condensate, and find that for strong impurity-bath interactions, the spectra narrow with increasing temperature, while the impurity energy shift is suppressed. Near the critical temperature for condensation, many-body effects still play an important role, and only for a nondegenerate bath the system approaches the classical Boltzmann-gas behavior. The key spectral features are reproduced within the theory of the ideal Bose polaron.
title: Fate of an Impurity Strongly Interacting with a Thermal Bose Gas

abstract: We report atomistic simulations of subcritical crack growth rates in silica glass that quantitatively align with experimental data. This result was achieved by a careful selection of simulation cell geometry and boundary conditions, a novel crack tip tracking algorithm, a robust interatomic potential that balances accuracy with computational efficiency, and high-performance parallel computing algorithms and resources. The simulations reveal a succession of burst-arrest events that produce subcritical crack growth across a broad range of rates, extending up to kilometers per second.
title: Atomistic Simulation of Subcritical Crack Growth in Glass in Vacuum

abstract: The world's first Compton scattering measurements on a $^3$He target were performed to probe neutron electromagnetic polarizabilities. Differential cross sections were measured at laboratory angles of $40^\circ$, $55^\circ$, $90^\circ$, $115^\circ$, $150^\circ$, using circularly polarized, quasi-monoenergetic photon beams at weighted mean energy values of 61.5 and 97.1 MeV from the High Intensity $γ$-ray Source at the Triangle Universities Nuclear Laboratory. Comparisons with chiral effective field theory show good agreement at 97.1 MeV but over-prediction at 61.5 MeV, motivating further theoretical development.
title: First Measurement of Compton Scattering on He 3 at HI γ S

abstract: Dissipation, though often detrimental to quantum entanglement, can be manipulated for the preparation of entangled states, wherein ingeniously designed quantum jump processes drive the system toward the desired steady state. Here we venture beyond this paradigm, and demonstrate a new type of entanglement generation in dissipative quantum dynamics. Combining driven-dissipative steady-state engineering and adiabatic passage, we propose a general protocol where the final entangled state depends on the chirality of the evolution path in the parameter space, a scheme that is further extendable to multipartite entanglement. By simulating the Liouvillian dynamics through the quantum Langevin equation for a pair of photons, we experimentally confirm the noise-resistant chiral preparation of various entangled states with high fidelity and concurrence. Our work establishes parametric chiral dynamics as a scalable and robust tool for controllable entanglement generation, paving the way for its applications in quantum information.
title: Chiral Entangled-State Generation through Dissipative Quantum Dynamics

abstract: Using the path-integral formalism, we show that photons possess a nontrivial quantum metric in momentum space. We derive the semiclassical action and equations of motion by taking into account the quantum metric. In media with a spatially varying refractive index $n(\mathbf{x})$, the quantum metric induces a shift in the trajectory of light at second order in derivatives of $n$, which may be regarded as a nonlinear Hall effect of light. The quantum metric also gives rise to corrections to gravitational lensing in curved spacetime at the nonlinear order in wavelength. This gravitational nonlinear Hall effect results from the interplay between the geometry of position space and that of momentum space.
title: Quantum metric and nonlinear Hall effect of photons

abstract: We show that Airy function partition functions for M2-brane theories may be derived from relative equivariant localization of quantum M-theory. The eleven-dimensional Chern–Simons coupling gives the cubic term in the grand potential, while the X 8 correction gives the charge shift. Fixing the M2-brane charge turns the localized M-theory path integral into an Airy integral. In this way we derive the ABJM result, its toric Calabi–Yau generalizations, and gravitational blocks for black holes and other spacetimes, up to the prefactor and non-perturbative corrections.
title: Airy functions from quantum M-theory

abstract: Framing anomaly is a key property of ( 2 + 1 ) d chiral topological orders, for it reveals that the chirality is an intrinsic bulk property of the system, rather than a property that requires a boundary between two systems. Understanding framing anomaly in lattice models is particularly interesting, as concrete, solvable lattice models of chiral topological orders are rare. In a previous work [Z.-A. Xu and J.-Y. Chen, .], we defined and solved the U(1) Chern-Simons-Maxwell theory on spacetime lattice, showing its chiral edge mode and the associated gravitational anomaly on boundary. In this Letter, we show its framing anomaly in the absence of boundary by computing the expectation of a lattice version of the modular T operator in the ground subspace on a spatial torus, from which we extract that ⟨ T ⟩ has a universal phase of − 2 π / 12 as expected: − 2 π / 8 from the Gauss-Milgram sum of the topological spins of the ground states, and 2 π / 24 from the framing anomaly. We can also extract the 2 π / 24 framing anomaly phase alone from the full spectrum of T in the ground subspace by computing ⟨ T m ⟩ . This pins down the last and most crucial property required for a valid lattice definition of U(1) Chern-Simons theory.
title: Framing Anomaly in Lattice Chern-Simons-Maxwell Theory

abstract: In homogeneous reversible chemical reactions, a prototypical nonequilibrium phenomenon, entropy-production fluctuations represent a sharper probe of nonequilibrium criticality than entropy-production response to variations in the chemical species concentrations.
title: Universal Criticality of Entropy Production in Chemical Reaction Networks

abstract: Axial splitting is the dominant failure mode of brittle solids under compression, yet its mechanical origin remains unclear. We show that clamped loading platens suppress lateral Poisson expansion, generating boundary-induced tensile stresses at the specimen interior -- the compressive analog of wrinkling in stretched sheets. This mechanism provides a predictive strength law, relating axial splitting to tensile strength, geometry, and confinement pressure. This is validated against diverse materials ranging from rocks to ceramics, establishing axial splitting as a geometry-controlled elastic process rather than a stochastic flaw problem.
title: Compressive Splitting in Brittle Solids: The Inverse of Wrinkling in Sheets

abstract: Electron-phonon coupling (EPC) plays a vital role in the electrical and optical properties of materials, ranging from superconductivity to charge dynamics. In moir'e superlattices, out-of-plane vibrations can modulate the moir'e potential and enhance interlayer EPC. Here we report the first direct observation of a resonance arising from coupling between moir'e electronic excitations and phonons in graphene-based moir'e superlattices. Using Fourier-transform infrared photocurrent spectroscopy, we detect the nominally silent hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) out-of-plane optical (ZO) phonon as a pronounced absorption peak. The phonon interferes with moir'e flat-band excitations to form a characteristic Fano resonance. Displacement field-dependent measurements confirm that the feature originates from coupling to the moir'e electronic continuum rather than simple zone folding. We further observe similar resonances in devices with different graphene layer numbers and twist configurations. This enhanced EPC provides a pathway for understanding and controlling emerging quantum phenomena, such as superconductivity, and engineering novel optoelectronic devices.
title: Moire-induced interlayer electron-phonon coupling in graphene/hBN superlattices

abstract: Chiral two-dimensional electron gases, which capture the electronic properties of graphene and rhombohedral graphene systems, exhibit singular momentum-space vortices and are susceptible to interaction-induced topological Haldane phases. Here, we investigate pairing interactions in the inversion-symmetric Haldane phases of chiral two-dimensional electron gases. We demonstrate that the nontrivial band topology of the Haldane phases enhances intravalley ($\mathbf{Q}=\ifmmode\pm\else\textpm\fi{}2{\mathbf{K}}_{D}$) pair susceptibility relative to intervalley ($\mathbf{Q}=0$) pair susceptibility, favoring the emergence of a lattice-scale pair-density wave order. When longitudinal acoustic phonons mediate the pairing interaction, the system supports a chiral Kekul\`e superconducting order at low densities. At higher densities, the phase diagram depends on the parity of the Chern number $J$. For even parity, an $s$-wave Kekul\`e order appears, while for odd parity we find a $\mathbf{Q}=0$ valley triplet chiral $J$ and a valley singlet $s$-wave order at different densities. Our findings are relevant to superconductivity in rhombohedral graphene and Kagome metals.
title: Kekulé Superconductivity Induced by Quantum Geometry in Haldane Phases

abstract: We present a closed formula for the computation of static post-Newtonian corrections to the two-body gravitational dynamics at any odd order, assuming the lower-order results are known. The formula is derived within a correlation function framework and exploits the Z 2 symmetry of the static sector, leading to a novel theoretical interpretation of the factorization theorem. As an application, we compute the gravitational interaction of two compact coalescing objects at the seventh post-Newtonian order in the static limit, which receives contributions from seven-loop graphs at order O ( G N 8 v 0 ) , and find complete agreement with the results obtained using the diagrammatic approach of the factorization theorem.
title: All-Order Structure of Static Gravitational Interactions and the Seventh Post-Newtonian Potential

abstract: Approximate quantum error correction (AQEC) provides a versatile framework for both quantum information processing and probing many-body entanglement. We reveal a fundamental tension between the error-correcting power of an AQEC and the hardness of code state preparation. More precisely, through a novel application of the Lovász local lemma, we establish a fundamental tradeoff between local indistinguishability and circuit complexity, showing that orthogonal short-range entangled states must be distinguishable via a local operator. These results offer a powerful tool for exploring quantum circuit complexity across diverse settings. As applications, we derive stronger constraints on the complexity of AQEC codes with transversal logical gates and establish strong complexity lower bounds for W state preparation. Our framework also provides a novel perspective for systems with Lieb-Schultz-Mattis type constraints.
title: Combinatorial Approach to Circuit Complexity: From Approximate Quantum Codes to Lieb-Schultz-Mattis Constraints

abstract: Identifying the transition pathway for ultrafast switching between distinct antiferromagnetic orders, while holding promise to realize unprecedentedly small and fast spin devices, remains largely unexplored. Herein, we show that rectifying structure with light can serve as a powerful tool to achieve nonthermal antiferromagnetic order switching in a monolayer antiferromagnet ${\mathrm{MnPSe}}_{3}$. By resolving the spin-phonon coupling strength, we identify a highly selective coupling of the magnetic order with a Raman-active ${\mathrm{E}}_{g}$ phonon. After resonantly pumping two degenerate infrared-active ${\mathrm{E}}_{u}$ modes, we obtain a new metastable out-of-equilibrium state holding shifted structure along the ${\mathrm{E}}_{g}$ mode. Such lattice distortion offers a sustained nonthermal driving field to trigger a phase switch from a N\'eel-type to a zigzag-type antiferromagnetic order within the coherent phonon lifetime. By varying the pumping polarization and intensity, we provide a parameter regime for realistic light-driven magnetic phase transitions. Such an ultrafast antiferromagnetism switch can be identified by pump-probe measurements of the order-parameter-like behavior in the second harmonic generation signal or absorption spectrum.
title: Terahertz Switching of Two-dimensional Antiferromagnetic Order

abstract: The realization of exciton-based quantum memories is fundamentally hindered by the trade-off between optical accessibility in bright states and long coherence lifetimes in dark states. While interlayer excitons offer promising lifetimes, their optical selection rules are typically locked by crystal symmetry, preventing dynamic switching via external fields. Here, we demonstrate a mechanism to deterministically toggle interlayer excitons between bright and dark states by leveraging sliding ferroelectricity within the framework of ferrovalley physics. By establishing a general symmetry criterion, we identify bilayer ${\mathrm{GeS}}_{2}$ as an ideal platform where interlayer sliding not only reverses the out-of-plane dipole but also rotates the optical principal axis by 90\ifmmode^\circ\else\textdegree\fi{}. Our calculations reveal that this structural reconfiguration switches the excitonic state at a specific valley from bright to dark for a fixed linear polarization, while simultaneously locking the excitation to a single valley. This establishes a nonvolatile and electrically reconfigurable coupling between ferroelectricity and excitonic optical activity, in which the bistable stacked structures encode different bright and dark exciton channels. These findings bridge ferroelectric control with exciton quantum optics, suggesting a viable path toward ultra-low-power optoelectronic memories and reconfigurable valleytronic routers.
title: Electrically Switchable Bright-Dark Excitons in Ferrovalley Bilayers

abstract: The longitudinal structure of the quark-gluon plasma (QGP) remains poorly constrained. Using a transport-model calculation of two-particle elliptic-flow correlations ${V}_{2\mathrm{\ensuremath{\Delta}}}(\mathrm{\ensuremath{\Delta}}\ensuremath{\eta})$ in relative pseudorapidity $\mathrm{\ensuremath{\Delta}}\ensuremath{\eta}$, we find two distinct initial-state components of flow decorrelation: a long-range component driven by the global geometry of participating nucleons and a short-range component reflecting local energy-deposition fluctuations. This short-range component extends to $|\mathrm{\ensuremath{\Delta}}\ensuremath{\eta}|\ensuremath{\sim}4$ and can be misidentified as final-state nonflow. For isobarlike nuclei with different shapes, the calculation predicts an experimentally testable fingerprint of this component: it dilutes the deformation contribution at small $|\mathrm{\ensuremath{\Delta}}\ensuremath{\eta}|$, so that the ${V}_{2\mathrm{\ensuremath{\Delta}}}(\mathrm{\ensuremath{\Delta}}\ensuremath{\eta})$ ratio between deformed and near-spherical systems, such as $\mathrm{U}+\mathrm{U}$-to-$\mathrm{Au}+\mathrm{Au}$, rises with $|\mathrm{\ensuremath{\Delta}}\ensuremath{\eta}|$. Separating long- and short-range flow decorrelations from nonflow gives access to the longitudinal initial structure and dynamics of the QGP.
title: Long-Range and Short-Range Longitudinal Flow Decorrelations in the Quark-Gluon Plasma

abstract: The excitation spectrum of fractional Chern insulators is identical to their fractional quantum Hall counterparts except for an enhancement factor, making it possible to predict their excitation spectrum from the Landau-level problem.
title: Similarity of Fractional Chern Insulators to Fractional Quantum Hall States: Moiré-Enhanced Gaps and Excitation-Spectrum Correspondence

abstract: Nonequilibrium equations of state can provide an effective thermodynamiclike description of far-from-equilibrium systems. We experimentally construct such an equation for a direct energy cascade in a turbulent two-dimensional Bose gas. Our homogeneous gas is continuously driven on a large length scale and, with matching dissipation on a small length scale, exhibits a nonthermal but stationary power-law momentum distribution. Our equation of state links the cascade amplitude with the underlying scale-invariant energy flux, and can, for different drive strengths, gas densities, and interaction strengths, be recast into a universal power-law form using scalings consistent with the Gross-Pitaevskii model.
title: Nonequilibrium Equation of State for a Turbulent 2D Bose Gas

abstract: Crystallization in polymers provides a fundamental probe of how molecular relaxation governs the emergence of order in glass-forming systems. Despite the longstanding success of the Lauritzen-Hoffman theory, its empirical treatment of molecular diffusion fails to capture the crystallization kinetics observed in the deeply supercooled regime. Here, we establish a physically grounded framework that replaces the empirical mobility in the Lauritzen-Hoffman formalism with a weighted combination of two measurable relaxation modes, namely the structural $\ensuremath{\alpha}$ relaxation, governing cooperative dynamics, and the slow Arrhenius process, associated with localized molecular rearrangements. This unified two-channel description quantitatively reproduces crystallization kinetics over several decades in time across 12 polymers spanning a wide range of fragility. In addition, our framework remains predictive under nanoconfinement, where interfaces and finite-size effects modify both mobility and nucleation. The results reveal that polymer crystallization proceeds through coupled long-range transport and localized ordering events governed by the same relaxation hierarchy that underlies vitrification, thus bridging glassy dynamics and crystallization kinetics at the molecular level.
title: Dual Relaxation Modes Control Polymer Crystallization

abstract: We develop a first-principles framework for evaluating the fundamental length scales of superconductivity, namely the coherence length $ξ_0$ and the magnetic penetration depth $λ_\mathrm{L}$, within superconducting density functional theory (SCDFT). By incorporating finite-momentum Cooper pairs, we formulate a microscopic scheme that enables a consistent and parameter-free determination of $ξ_0$, $λ_\mathrm{L}$, and the superconducting transition temperature $T_\mathrm{c}$ on the same theoretical footing. Applying the method to representative elemental superconductors, the A15 compound V$_3$Si, and H$_3$S under high pressure, we obtain results in good agreement with available experimental and reproduce the type-I/type-II classification across all materials studied. The unified access to $ξ_0$ and $λ_\mathrm{L}$ further allows us to construct the Uemura plot entirely from first principles, showing that higher-$T_\mathrm{c}$ systems are characterized by the simultaneous realization of strong pairing and large phase stiffness. Our results establish a predictive first-principles route to superconducting length scales and provide a microscopic interpretation of empirical correlations in superconductivity.
title: First-Principles Calculation of Coherence Length and Penetration Depth Based on Density Functional Theory for Superconductors

abstract: Relaxation of far-from-equilibrium quantum fluids, intimately related to the emergence of long-range order, is theoretically associated with the decay of a turbulent isotropic tangle of vortex lines. We observe and study such decaying quantum turbulence in a homogeneous 3D atomic Bose gas. Using matter-wave techniques to magnify the gas density distribution, and then imaging a thin slice of the magnified cloud, we observe imprints of randomly oriented vortex lines and measure the vortex-line-length density L . The observed decay of L agrees with the prediction for Vinen “ultraquantum” turbulence. Although our weakly interacting gases are highly compressible, their large-scale dynamics are consistent with the behavior of an incompressible hydrodynamic fluid, with the decay of L not depending on the strength of the interatomic interactions and being similar to that in the strongly interacting superfluid helium.
title: Observation of Vinen Turbulence during Far-from-Equilibrium Bose-Einstein Condensation

abstract: Ultralow thermal conductivity ($\ensuremath{\kappa}$) underpins thermal insulation and nonequilibrium energy conversion at large temperature gradients. In compositionally pure amorphous silicon with predominantly tetrahedral coordination, a conventional benchmark for minimum thermal conductivity is provided by the Cahill-Watson-Pohl model, which constrains the phonon mean free path to half the wavelength. Here, we show an anomalously low $\ensuremath{\kappa}$ down to $0.67\text{ }\text{ }\mathrm{W}/\mathrm{mK}$ at 300 K, about 33% below this conventional Cahill-Watson-Pohl benchmark, in amorphous Si obtained via high-pressure phase engineering. By combining the unified heat-transport framework with molecular dynamics simulations, we attribute the ultralow $\ensuremath{\kappa}$ to unusually undercoordinated Si sites generated by rapid mechanical quenching from high pressure. These sites generate inhomogeneous local force fields and seed rattlinglike lattice dynamics, leading to strong anharmonicity and vibrational-mode localization. Our results offer a microscopic blueprint for engineering solids with anomalously low $\ensuremath{\kappa}$ through undercoordination in amorphous networks, without introducing alloying or complex-unit-cell architectures.
title: Anomalously Low Thermal Conductivity in Undercoordinated Amorphous Silicon

abstract: We perform an amplitude analysis of the decay $D^0 \to K_S^0 π^0 η$ and measure its absolute branching fraction to be $(1.016 \pm 0.013_{\text {stat.}} \pm 0.014_{\text {syst.}})\%$. The analysis utilizes $20.3~\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$ of $e^{+}e^{-}$ collision data collected at a center-of-mass energy of 3.773~GeV with the BESIII detector. The branching fraction of the intermediate process $D^0 \rightarrow \bar{K}^*(892)^0 η$ is determined to be $(0.73 \pm 0.05_{\text {stat.}} \pm 0.03_{\text {syst.}}) \%$, which is $5 σ$ smaller than the result measured in $D^0 \to K^- π^+ η$ by the Belle experiment. As a result, the magnitudes of the $W$-exchange and QCD-penguin exchange amplitudes are found to be less than half of their current estimations. Furthermore, we determine $\mathcal{B}(D^0\to K_S^0a_0(980)^0, a_0(980)^0\to π^0η) = (9.88\pm 0.37_{\rm stat.}\pm 0.42_{\rm syst.})\times10^{-3}$, with a precision improved by a factor of 4.5 compared to the world average.
title: Study of K S 0 a 0 ( 980 ) 0 and K ‾ * ( 892 ) 0 η in the D 0 → K S 0 π 0 η decay

abstract: We track individual grains during the discharge of a quasi-2D silo and measure their instantaneous acceleration. This reveals collective deceleration waves which propagate upward through the packing, even though the outlet flow rate remains steady and follows the Beverloo law. Their characteristic frequency shows no systematic trend with aperture size and scales as $\sqrt{g/d}$. We model this scaling with a minimal stick-slip model along the dead zones, in which the relevant length scale is the grain diameter $d$. Introducing anisotropic magnetic interactions promote the formation of vertically aligned grain chains, which increase the characteristic length scale along the flow direction while leaving the transverse size nearly unchanged. This anisotropic elongation leads to a systematic decrease in wave frequency. Our results demonstrate that the internal flow is fundamentally intermittent and governed by grain-scale physics, in sharp contrast with the steady, aperture-controlled flow at the outlet.
title: Grain-Scale Origin of Stick-Slip Waves in Silo Discharge: Influence of Cohesion

abstract: Three-dimensional topological ferroelectric (3D-TFE) insulators, in which topological and ferroelectric orders naturally coexist, enable field-controlled spintronic devices. In this Letter, we predict a previously unknown structure of bismuth monohalides ${\text{Bi}}_{4}{X}_{4}$ ($X=\mathrm{Br}$, I), denoted the $\ensuremath{\gamma}$ phase, and demonstrate that it is an ideal 3D-TFE insulator. Systematic first-principles calculations confirm the stability and synthesizability of $\ensuremath{\gamma}\text{\ensuremath{-}}{\text{Bi}}_{4}{X}_{4}$. Although the noncentrosymmetric $\ensuremath{\gamma}$ phase crystallizes in the space group $Cmc{2}_{1}$ with no symmetry-based classifications or indicators, the nontrivial topology can be characterized by the nonzero spin Chern number. Moreover, the $z$-direction polarization can be switched by interlayer sliding with a small energy barrier. Finally, we design an electrically controlled spin-filter device that can generate a switchable spin-polarized current. Combining a single-phase crystal, a sizable band gap, and robust band topology against ferroelectric switching, these bismuth monohalides serve as a prototype of intrinsic 3D-TFE insulators, providing an ideal platform for realizing new nonvolatile functionalities in spintronic devices.
title: Three-Dimensional Topological Ferroelectrics

abstract: Finite-frequency nonlocal conductivity calculations show that clean 2D Fermi liquids in the tomographic regime realize a dynamical universality class distinct from the conventional Navier--Stokes paradigm.
title: ac Fingerprints of 2D Electron Hydrodynamics: Superdiffusion and Drude Weight Suppression

abstract: Cellular adaptation operates far from equilibrium. It is governed by the nonequilibrium driving force. Yet how these nonequilibrium dynamics quantitatively determine the trade-offs among speed, robustness, and cost remains unclear. Using the yeast pheromone response as a model system, we develop a unified framework linking adaptation kinetics, nonequilibrium characteristics, and landscape topology. Our analysis reveals synchronized biphasic responses across these domains, marked by landscape flattening, pathway convergence, and elevated thermodynamic dissipation. Across the pheromone-dose crossover, the system shifts from fast, distributed adaptation with reduced dissipation to slow, robust dynamics stabilized by dominant pathways. By integrating dynamics with thermodynamics, this framework quantifies the thermodynamic and topological constraints of cellular decision-making, providing a generalizable strategy for dissecting adaptation across complex biological systems.
title: Nonequilibrium Biphasic Response and Speed-Robustness-Cost Trade-offs in Cellular Adaptation

abstract: Measuring part of a quantum system in the midst of its evolution and acting on the result in real time is essential for numerous quantum information protocols. Neutral-atom arrays are a leading platform for quantum information processing, but their midcircuit measurement-and-feedforward cycle times have remained slow, typically exceeding 1 ms. Here, we demonstrate fast midcircuit measurement and real-time feedforward in an array of atomic qubits coupled to a high-finesse optical cavity. Local light shifts tune individual data qubits out of resonance with the cavity, shielding their coherence, while a near-resonant probe drives a selected qubit whose emission is collected with Purcell enhancement. Midcircuit measurements of four qubits with subpercent infidelity reduce the coherence of a fifth unmeasured data qubit by less than 2%. We implement real-time feedforward to correct measurement-induced phase shifts and to realize an adaptive circuit for optimal quantum-state discrimination and conditional state preparation. Our approach reduces the measurement-and-feedforward cycle time to below $100\text{ }\text{ }\mathrm{\ensuremath{\mu}}\mathrm{s}$ and establishes optical cavities as a route to fast control of neutral-atom quantum systems.
title: Rapid Cavity-Based Midcircuit Measurement and Feedforward in a Neutral Atom Array

abstract: Chiral spin liquid (CSL) is a magnetic analogue of the fractional quantum Hall (FQH) liquid. Collective excitations play a vital role in shaping our understanding of these exotic quantum phases of matter and their quantum phase transitions. While the magneto-roton and long-wavelength chiral graviton modes in the FQH and fractional Chern insulator (FCI) liquids have been extensively explored, whether CSLs host analogous or qualitatively different modes remains elusive. Here we explore the collective excitations in the SU(2) symmetric CSL phase. Combining exact diagonalization and time-dependent variational principle calculations, we identify two spin-singlet collective modes: a chiral p-wave roton mode at finite momentum, and a elliptically polarized d-wave nematic mode at zero momentum, both of which are prominent across the CSL phase. The chiral p-wave singlet roton has no counterpart in FQH of FCI systems, and the q = 0 d-wave mode also exhibits fingerprint distinct from those of FQH/FCI liquids. We also elucidate that both singlet modes are general for CSLs on various lattice models. By tuning J2, we find the nematic mode to be pronouncedly soft, together with the spin-triplet two-spinon bound states, potentially promoting strong nematic and spin stripe instabilities. Our work paves the way for further understanding CSL from the dynamical perspective and provides new spectroscopic signatures for future experiments of CSL candidates.
title: Collective excitations in chiral spin liquid: Chiral roton and long-wavelength nematic mode

abstract: Point-gap bound states in non-Hermitian systems are generally expected to lose their purely impurity-localized character under open boundary conditions (OBC) owing to hybridization with the non-Hermitian skin effect (NHSE). Here, we demonstrate that such states can retain impurity localization in a one-dimensional non-Hermitian continuum, even after point-gap collapse under OBC. The mechanism is a non-Bloch standing wave established between the impurity and a boundary, which suppresses the skin-accumulating components. Experimentally, we use a programmable piezoelectric actuator array mounted on an elastic beam to introduce non-Hermiticity and directly observe the predicted OBC-persistent point-gap bound state. Our results establish a route for preserving impurity localization against NHSE hybridization.
title: Open-Boundary-Condition-Persistent Point-Gap Bound States in the Non-Hermitian Continuum

abstract: A central challenge in turbulence research is understanding the physics underlying the nonlinear interactions between scales of motion. In addition to this multiscale behavior, wall-bounded turbulence supports inhomogeneous structures in the wall-normal direction. We extend the classical spectral (scale-to-scale) turbulence energy cascade, which lacks spatial localization, by introducing the spatiotemporal-spectral (STS) cascade that incorporates wall-normal structure to the spectral description. This spatiotemporal adaptation is energy conserving and suggests very-large-scale motions provide the architecture to support both wall-normal and spectral energy transfer. In this Letter, we show that despite their energetic dominance, very-large-scale motions play a passive role in the energy exchange and instead link the inner and outer flow regions through phase synchronization while facilitating energy transfer.
title: Spatiotemporal Architecture of Energy Transfer in Wall-Bounded Turbulence

abstract: The uncertain mass distribution of stars and compact objects in the galactic center significantly alter the timing uncertainty of the observed pulses from the pulsar orbiting the supermassive black hole at the center of our galaxy.
title: Granular Mass Perturbations on the Pulsar-Supermassive Black Hole System

abstract: Photon antibunching in resonance fluorescence - the emission from a single, resonantly driven two-level quantum emitter - is a paradigmatic signature of nonclassical light. Photon entanglement, by contrast, manifests as correlations that can defy any classical description and is typically regarded as a distinct quantum effect. Here, we experimentally extract pairs of narrowband, time-bin–entangled photons from the antibunched resonance fluorescence of a single trapped atom. We verify entanglement by using the CHSH Bell inequality as an entanglement witness and by reconstructing the two-photon density matrix. The observed correlations vanish when the coincidence time window exceeds the antibunching timescale, revealing underlying multimode entanglement in the emitted field. Our results establish a direct link between photon antibunching and photon–photon entanglement, connecting two canonical signatures of nonclassical light.
title: Relationship between antibunching and entanglement in resonance fluorescence

abstract: The breakup of thinning (stretching) liquid filaments is strongly influenced by localized perturbations arising from impurities or suspended particles. Using numerical simulations and analytical modelling, we investigate the role of a solid particle on the breakup dynamics of a stretching liquid filament. We show that particle-induced perturbations trigger a universal pinch-off dynamics in the viscous regime. Once the filament surface approaches the particle, the subsequent breakup becomes self-similar and independent of the particle size. We derive an analytical expression for the pinch-off time based on the interplay between filament stretching and Rayleigh–Plateau instability, which agrees quantitatively with simulations. Our results reveal a universal mechanism by which localized perturbations control the breakup of viscous filaments containing solid particles.
title: Self-similar breakup of a viscous liquid filament with a solid particle

abstract: We show that Anderson localization fundamentally reshapes dissipative superconducting electrodynamics, replacing the linear Mattis--Bardeen pair-breaking onset with a parametrically weaker quadratic Mott edge while leaving the quasiparticle spectrum unchanged. We derive this behavior for a weakly disordered single-channel wire with a spatially uniform $s$-wave pair potential using a Nambu-space extension of the Berezinskii diagram technique that resums elastic impurity scattering to all orders. Conservation of the Bogoliubov branch collapses the Nambu diagram hierarchy onto an exactly solvable localization problem. The localization length remains equal to its normal-state value, whereas the localization time diverges at the gap edge. The new absorption edge results from the product of the superconducting pair-creation coherence factor and the Mott-suppressed current matrix elements between localized orbitals, which generates the characteristic double logarithm. Localization also reduces the Hebel--Slichter coherence peak. The resulting theory provides an all-orders benchmark for microwave and spin-relaxation experiments on localized superconducting nanowires.
title: Quadratic pair-breaking absorption edge from Anderson localization in a superconducting wire

abstract: Electrons photoemitted by strong laser fields can rescatter, generating attosecond high harmonics. Spectral peaks arise from inter- and intracycle interference of coherent electron wave packets. While intercycle interference is well known, intracycle interference of plateau electrons has not been observed. We present carrier-envelope phase-resolved photoemission spectra from a nanometric tungsten needle tip driven at 1570 nm revealing such interference, supported by quantum orbit and TDSE simulations that elucidate attosecond-scale electron dynamics.
title: Intracycle Interference in Strong-Field Photoemission from a Tungsten Needle Tip

abstract: Competing electric dipole orders arising from nearly degenerate free-energy landscapes underpin a broad range of emergent functionalities in complex oxides yet remain largely unexplored in two-dimensional van der Waals materials. Here, we report direct evidence for the coexistence of polar and antipolar states in niobium oxide dichloride under ambient conditions. Through concerted microscopic structural characterization and mesoscopic domain imaging in conjunction with first-principles calculations, we establish that the two dipole-ordered phases are nearly degenerate in energy and form intricately intertwined domain structures across multiple length scales. We further demonstrate a reversible, strain-driven transition from the antiferroelectric to the ferroelectric state under continuous in situ uniaxial tensile strain, revealing an exceptionally flat energy landscape and strong susceptibility to mechanical stimulus. The strain response further suggests an intimate coupling between electric dipole order and the Peierls distortion of the quasi-one-dimensional Nb-Nb chains, linking ionic polarization to the underlying electronic structure. Together with the isolated flat band in niobium oxide dichloride, these findings establish a promising platform for exploring strain-programmable ferroic functionalities and ferroelectric control of correlated electronic states in van der Waals materials.
title: Strain-Tunable Competing Polar Orders in NbOCl 2

abstract: Quantum simulation offers a powerful approach to studying quantum field theories, particularly ( 2 + 1 ) D quantum electrodynamics ( QED 3 ) with Wilson fermions, which hosts a rich landscape of physical phenomena. A key challenge in lattice formulations is the proper realization of topological phases and the Chern-Simons terms, where fermion discretization plays a crucial role. In this Letter, we highlight the differences between staggered and Wilson fermions coupled to U(1) gauge fields in the Hamiltonian formulation. We analyze why staggered fermions fail to induce ( 2 + 1 ) D topological phases, while Wilson fermions admit a variety of topological phases including Chern insulator and quantum spin Hall phases. Additionally, we uncover a rich phase diagram for the two-flavor Wilson fermion model in the presence of a chemical potential. Our findings resolve existing ambiguities in Hamiltonian formulations and provide a theoretical foundation for future quantum simulations of lattice field theories with topological phases. We further outline connections to experimental platforms, offering guidance for implementations on near-term quantum computing architectures. A complementary presentation of the analytical calculations, the identification of robust topological structure and response, and extensive numerical results is contained in a joint submission [S. Bharadwaj , , 094502 (2026)].
title: Path to Quantum Simulations of Topological Phases: ( 2 + 1 ) D Quantum Electrodynamics with Wilson Fermions

abstract: Anomalous ferroelectric-like electronic hysteresis has recently been reported in intrinsically nonpolar graphene/hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) heterostructures and widely exploited to realize electrically switchable superconductivity, correlated insulators, and neuromorphic functionalities. The origin of this anomalous hysteresis is still under debate, hindering its applications. Among the proposals are moiré-driven charge transfer, twist angles between hBN, conductive sliding ferroelectricity and dielectric defects. Here we study the detailed hysteretic transport properties in dual-gated hBN/graphene/hBN heterostructures. Two devices that share the same moiré and twist angle configurations exhibit strikingly distinct hysteretic responses, allowing us to unambiguously rule out moiré-induced and twist-angle-related mechanisms. Moreover, the ratchet-like charge injections give rise to unconventional hysteresis that is pronouncedly asymmetric and continuously scalable with the sweeping range of external electric fields, in sharp contrast to conventional ferroelectric behavior with fixed coercive fields that is symmetric with respect to zero field. These observations challenge the theoretical scenario in terms of spontaneous interlayer electrical polarizations and lead us to consider the defects within hBN flakes. Our analysis and simulations suggest that the interplay between the defects and conducting channel plays an important role in inducing the ratchet-like charge injections and anomalous hysteresis. Our work provides more insight in the origin of electronic hysteresis in graphene-based van der Waals heterostructures, and the observations of asymmetric and scalable electronic hysteresis could lead to new-generation ultrafast memory and synaptic devices.
title: Asymmetric and Scalable Electronic Hysteresis Induced by Ratchet-like Charge Injections in van der Waals Heterostructures

abstract: Liquid interfaces and membranes represent two physically opposite regimes of interfacial dynamics: the former are governed by interfacial tension, while the latter are governed by bending elasticity. What happens when these two extremes are combined by confining a coacervate liquid within a membrane geometry is a largely unexplored question. Here, we probe the membrane dynamics of polyelectrolyte complex vesicles with coacervate cores using neutron spin echo spectroscopy. The relaxation rate follows $\mathrm{\ensuremath{\Gamma}}\ensuremath{\sim}{q}^{3}$ (where $q$ denotes the magnitude of the scattering vector), demonstrating that bending undulations prevail despite the intrinsically liquid nature of the constituents. However, the reduced relaxation rate ${\ensuremath{\eta}}_{0}\mathrm{\ensuremath{\Gamma}}/{k}_{\mathrm{B}}T$ (where ${\ensuremath{\eta}}_{0}$ and ${k}_{\mathrm{B}}T$ denote the solvent viscosity and thermal energy, respectively) is more than an order of magnitude higher than that of lipid bilayers, despite the fourfold larger membrane thickness, indicating an exceptionally weak bending restoring force. This quantity remains invariant across temperatures and salt concentrations, indicating that the bending elasticity is entropic in origin. Thus, the geometric constraint of the vesicular structure imposes bending-undulation dynamics on an otherwise liquid interface while preserving the entropy-driven nature of the coacervate.
title: When Liquids Form Membranes: Entropy-Dominated Bending Dynamics in Coacervate Vesicles

abstract: Pulsars are difficult to discover via γ -ray pulsations because typically only one photon is observed per ∼ 10 8 rotations. We report the first γ -ray pulsar discovered with an extension of a recently proposed algorithm, which uses efficient tools for identifying short vectors in high-dimensional lattices instead of exhaustively searching for periodic signals. PSR J1622 − 7204, an isolated pulsar spinning at 261 Hz, was found in 15 years of Fermi-LAT data using about ten CPU hours. In contrast, the previous state-of-the-art (a semicoherent search) failed after ∼ 600 CPU years. This new approach may enable the discovery of many new γ -ray pulsars, including in binary systems, a previously intractable problem without detailed prior knowledge of the orbital parameters.
title: Gamma-Ray Pulsar Discovery Using a Lattice-Based Method

abstract: Ultrafast pump-probe spectroscopy is indispensable for investigating interactions, collective excitations, and nonequilibrium dynamics in superconductors and correlated electron systems. However, how a small gap opening near the Fermi surface affects the spectral changes in the high-energy interband transition region remains elusive. To address this issue, we perform systematic studies of carrier relaxation dynamics in the prototype charge-density-wave (CDW) material ${\mathrm{EuAl}}_{4}$. We find that the CDW gap shrinks substantially under optical pumping. This band renormalization strongly modulates interband transitions associated with the gap edge, inducing a pronounced transient reflectivity change at the corresponding probe energies. These results establish a direct link between low-energy order-parameter dynamics and high-energy spectral responses, providing a general framework for interpreting transient signals in gapped quantum materials.
title: Unveiling High-Energy Ultrafast Responses Driven by Fermi-Level Gap Opening in Charge-Density Waves

abstract: Noise and errors are unavoidable in any realistic quantum process, including processes designed to reduce noise and errors in the first place. In particular, quantum thermodynamical protocols for cooling can be significantly affected, potentially altering both their performance and efficiency. Analytically characterizing the impact of such errors becomes increasingly challenging as the system size grows, particularly in deep quantum circuits where noise can accumulate in complex ways. To address this, we introduce a general framework for approximating the cumulative effect of gate-dependent noise using a global depolarizing channel. We specify the regime in which this approximation provides a reliable description of the noisy dynamics. Applying our framework to the thermodynamical two-sort algorithmic cooling (TSAC) protocol, we analytically derive its asymptotic cooling limit in the presence of noise. Using the cooling limit, the optimal cooling performance is achieved by a finite number of qubits—distinguished from the conventional noiseless TSAC protocol by an infinite number of qubits—and fundamental bounds on the achievable ground-state population are derived. This approach opens new avenues for exploring noisy quantum thermodynamical processes.
title: Exploring Noisy Quantum Thermodynamical Processes via the Depolarizing-Channel Approximation

abstract: We resolve the long-standing claim that regularization by dimensional reduction (DR) fails to preserve supersymmetry in supersymmetric Yang–Mills (SYM) theories at three loops. Earlier results reported a mismatch between the Yukawa and ghost-gluon β functions in N = 2 SYM, suggesting a breakdown of supersymmetry. We show that this discrepancy does not originate from DR itself but from subtleties in the treatment of the Clifford algebra. A corrected three-loop calculation restores full supersymmetric behavior, and we demonstrate that the same issue would first affect N = 4 SYM only at five loops, consistent with existing four-loop results. Our findings confirm that DR preserves supersymmetry for N = 1 , 2 , and 4 SYM through the loop orders examined.
title: Dimensional Reduction Is Supersymmetric at Three Loops

abstract: Topology under non-Hermitian dynamics is encoded in the phase of the bulk evolution, yet strong dissipation suppresses the amplitudes carrying it. We resolve this using a programmable photonic integrated circuit that implements such dynamics in synthetic momentum space through unitary dilation, with the phase recovered by phase-shifted interferometry. For the non-Hermitian Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, the method distinguishes trivial and nontrivial Zak phases and yields a coherence winding q = ± 1 induced by an exceptional point. Extending to a synthetic torus via a Rice-Mele pump gives the first Chern number Ch 1 = 0 , 1 for trivial and nontrivial cycles, showing a programmable route to momentum-space topology under strongly dissipative non-Hermitian dynamics.
title: Interferometric Readout of Momentum-Space Topology in a Programmable Dissipative Photonic Circuit

abstract: Ultrahigh continuous-wave intensities $(>300\text{ }\text{ }\mathrm{GW}/{\mathrm{cm}}^{2})$ in high-numerical-aperture optical cavities enable applications from phase-contrast electron microscopy to ultradeep dipole traps for molecules. However, the intensity can be limited by the optomechanical parametric instability (PI), where mirror vibrations scatter light from one cavity mode into another. We observe parametric instability in a tabletop Fabry-P\'erot cavity, show that the mechanical modes are MHz-frequency bulk acoustic modes inside the mirrors, and measure their $Q$ factor. By using low-$Q$ mirrors, we achieve $>500\text{ }\text{ }\mathrm{GW}/{\mathrm{cm}}^{2}$ intensities in an open, free-space cavity.
title: Optomechanical Limit on Intracavity Intensities from Bulk Mirror Vibrations

abstract: A GAGG:Ce crystal scintillator contaminated by thorium was used to search for double-$\ensuremath{\alpha}$ decay of $^{224}\mathrm{Ra}$. Considering that the daughter nucleus is $^{216}\mathrm{Po}$ with the half-life of 0.144 s, the time-amplitude method was utilized to search for $^{224}\mathrm{Ra}$ $2\ensuremath{\alpha}$ events, which allows for a significant background reduction in the region of the expected effect. No double-$\ensuremath{\alpha}$ decay events were observed, allowing us to set a lower limit on the decay half-life, $\mathrm{lim}{T}_{1/2}=64\text{ }\text{ }\mathrm{yr}$ at 90% confidence level, which exceeds the theoretical predictions of the symmetric model of $2\ensuremath{\alpha}$ decay (${T}_{1/2}=2.6\text{ }\text{ }\mathrm{yr}$).
title: Lower Limit on the Double-Alpha Decay of Ra 224

abstract: We present perturbative quantum chromodynamics (pQCD) predictions for the modification to the yield of high-momentum particles in very light ion collisions---$^{10}\mathrm{B}+^{10}\mathrm{B}$, $^{6}\mathrm{Li}+^{6}\mathrm{Li}$, $^{4}\mathrm{He}+^{4}\mathrm{He}$, and $^{3}\mathrm{He}+^{3}\mathrm{He}$---both with and without medium-induced energy loss. We show that there is nontrivial suppression expected from our partonic energy loss model in symmetric systems from $^{208}\mathrm{Pb}+^{208}\mathrm{Pb}$ to $^{3}\mathrm{He}+^{3}\mathrm{He}$ and in asymmetric systems $A+B$, and that the energy loss scales approximately with $(\sqrt{AB}{)}^{1/3}$. Further, we find that deep inelastic scattering measurements in $^{3}\mathrm{He}$ and $^{6}\mathrm{Li}$ tightly constrain the nPDF baseline, making these isotopes a particularly clean environment for searching for final-state partonic energy loss induced by the formation of a quark-gluon plasma in these very small systems.
title: From Lead to Helium: Potential for a Measurement of Jet Quenching in the Smallest Collision Systems

abstract: The local-operator entanglement (LOE) measures the classical simulability of a Heisenberg operator and is conjectured to witness many-body chaos in locally interacting systems. Using tools from free probability, we analytically compute its asymptotic value for Haar random dynamics for all R\'enyi indices. We find that to the first two orders in large dimension, for traceless operators it exactly reproduces the Page curve for random states. In contrast to higher-order out-of-time-ordered correlators, which depend on more complex operator correlations via free cumulants, the leading-order LOE is independent of the initial operator. We detail exactly how these higher-order correlations are encoded in the coefficients of the finite-size corrections. Guided by our Haar result, we argue that the long-time value of the LOE entropies in chaotic systems is robust: they depend only on a simple subsector of the hierarchy of correlations encoded by the full eigenstate thermalization hypothesis. Our results therefore provide a conceptual boundary between operator simulability and higher-order scrambling diagnostics.
title: Page Curve for Local-Operator Entanglement from Free Probability

abstract: Interstitial atoms such as oxygen, carbon, and nitrogen are common point defects in crystalline solids and play important roles in determining electronic and mechanical properties. For decades, their behavior has been modeled assuming random spatial distributions owing to the lack of direct experimental access to their atomic-scale arrangements. Here, using oxygen-doped α-titanium as a model system, we overcome this fundamental limitation by achieving the first three-dimensional visualization, quantitative counting, and sub-[˚]Angstr¨om positioning of individual interstitial oxygen atoms in the bulk, enabled by super-resolution 4D-STEM ptychography with an adaptive prop agator. We find that interstitial oxygen atoms do not distribute randomly; instead, they exhibit correlated occupancy along the [0001] direction, giving rise to nanoscale ordered domains that are not detectable by conventional imaging. This discovery overturns the long-standing paradigm of randomness in interstitial systems and provides a microscopic foundation for understanding anomalous transport, strengthening, and phase stability in interstitial-engineered materials. Our approach establishes a general platform for atomic-scale defect metrology, opening avenues to ratio nally design materials through precise control of interstitial architectures in metals, semiconductors, and quantum solids.
title: Ordering of oxygen atoms in titanium revealed by superresolution electron ptychography

abstract: We propose a classification scheme for rotational bands built on nuclear scissors vibrations, based on a systematic analysis of the competition among distinct collective modes. Our analysis within the proton-neutron interacting boson model reveals that scissors-mode bands exhibit robust odd-even staggering in excitation energies, leading to multiple energy-splitting patterns in scissors rotations. Remarkably, despite their distinct origins, these splitting patterns share a common spectroscopic fingerprint: pronounced clustering between the two lowest band members with spin-parity ${1}^{+}$ and ${2}^{+}$. This behavior naturally accounts for the puzzlingly small separation between the two levels observed in $^{156}\mathrm{Gd}$ and establishes a general mechanism applicable to axially asymmetric nuclei and, potentially, to other two-fluid systems exhibiting scissors-mode collectivity. We also present theoretical predictions for the systematic evolution of this splitting across the deformed Gd isotopic chain, further corroborating the proposed mechanism.
title: Classification of Scissors Rotational Bands in Deformed Nuclei

abstract: Coulomb interactions underpin the formation of excitons, yet their role in nonequilibrium exciton relaxation has remained unexplored. Here, using first-principles real-time Bethe-Salpeter formalism combined with nonadiabatic molecular dynamics, we study the ultrafast relaxation of optically bright excitons into momentum-dark states in monolayer ${\mathrm{WSe}}_{2}$. It is demonstrated that Coulomb-mediated couplings between excitonic configurations are strictly forbidden in a perfect lattice but are dynamically activated by phonon excitation. This activation enables the long-range Coulomb interaction to dominate exciton relaxation, reshaping kinetic pathways and surpassing conventional electron-phonon scattering. These findings reveal a new paradigm in which Coulomb interactions actively govern nonequilibrium exciton kinetics, while phonons act as a dynamical switch that unlocks many-body relaxation channels.
title: Many-Body-Driven Ultrafast Exciton Relaxation Enabled by Phonon-Activated Coulomb Coupling

abstract: Childhood adversity increases the risk of chronic pain and anxiety later in life, particularly in women, yet the neural mechanisms linking early-life stress to adult vulnerability remain elusive. Here, we show that social isolation and nerve injury interact to amplify activity-dependent synaptic gain and anticipatory recruitment of the paraventricular thalamus-to-central amygdala pathway in female, but not male, mice. This female-specific circuit sensitization enhances mechanical hypersensitivity and avoidance behaviors in adulthood. Chemogenetic pathway inhibition selectively rescued these behaviors when stress and injury co-occurred, whereas sustained and phasic pathway activation triggered mechanical hypersensitivity and avoidance, respectively. Together, these findings uncovered a latent thalamo-amygdalar synaptic gain state that is unmasked by a subsequent injury and transforms early-life stress into female-specific vulnerability to chronic pain and anxiety-like avoidance.
title: A thalamo-amygdalar circuit drives female vulnerability to chronic pain after early-life stress

abstract: Pacific salmon are depleted due to anthropogenic impacts, and populations have failed to recover despite management interventions. Predation on salmon by pinnipeds and seabirds has been suggested as a barrier to recovery, leading to calls for predator culls by some. However, no studies have evaluated the whole-ecosystem impact of removing these predators nor estimated the direct and indirect effects of these culls on salmon. We use an end-to-end ecosystem model to assess the efficacy of widespread culls in marine environments. We find that culls are unlikely to benefit salmon due to the indirect food web effects of predator reduction and the low biomass of top predator groups. Instead, more abundant fish predators, northward-expanding competitors, and temperature-sensitive prey have larger effects on salmon in the ocean.
title: Widespread marine mammal and seabird reductions are unlikely to benefit salmon due to indirect ecosystem effects

abstract: Recent trends reverse progress toward zero-deforestation.
title: Rising risk of deforestation in Indonesia’s pulp sector

abstract: Quantum phenomena can be exploited to tackle certain problems beyond the reach of classical approaches. In this study, we focus on coordinated decision-making among many players without communication, the study of which, on current quantum processors, has remained elusive. Using a superconducting qubit processor, we show that quantum contextuality enables certain tasks to be performed with success probabilities beyond classical limits. With a few qubits, we illustrate quantum contextuality with the magic square game and quantify it through a Bell-Kochen-Specker inequality violation. To examine many-body contextuality, we implement the N -player Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger game and separately solve a two-dimensional hidden linear function problem, advancing the state of the art on fidelity and system size in both tasks. Our work introduces benchmarking of quantum processors using contextuality-based algorithms.
title: Quantum-classical separation in bounded-resource tasks arising from measurement contextuality

abstract: Redox-mediated chemistry is central to both the biosynthesis and cytotoxicity of many natural products, yet how microbes balance these processes remains poorly understood. Here, we uncover a conserved mechanism that coordinates three redox-mediated processes in secondary metabolite biosynthesis: self-protection, prevention of substrate degradation, and late-stage biosynthesis. Using the antitumor antibiotic doxorubicin as a model system, we show that the vicinal oxygen chelate (VOC) protein DnrV prevents reactive oxygen species formation and substrate degradation while promoting P450 catalysis. We expand this paradigm to a conserved family of VOC-fold proteins, redox-associated cytotoxin-binding proteins (REACT), found across bacteria, fungi, and plants. REACT represents a multifunctional protein class that balances antibiotic assembly, self-protection, and prevention of metabolite destruction, providing a foundational understanding of production of redox-active natural products.
title: Balancing redox-mediated cytotoxicity and catalysis in natural product biosynthesis

abstract: Although RNA quality control tightly regulates gene expression, the scope of its regulatory functions in the nucleus remains unclear. In this study, we describe the quality control, on chromatin, of poised intron-containing polyadenylated RNAs (PIA-RNAs). Whether these precursor messenger RNAs (pre-mRNAs) constitute immature mRNAs whose splicing is pending or, alternatively, are degraded by the nuclear RNA exosome depends on whether they engage nuclear cap-binding protein 3 (NCBP3) or anillin, respectively. Many PIA-RNAs inversely controlled by NCBP3 and anillin encode mitochondrial factors. Thus, NCBP3 depletion in mouse as well as pathogenic mutations in the RNA exosome in humans result in reduced mitochondrial activity, muscle weakness, cerebellar hypomyelination, and diminished motor coordination. Our findings reveal a competition between pre-mRNA metabolic pathways whose balance controls mitochondrial function and, when perturbed, leads to neurological diseases.
title: The fate of poised pre-mRNAs shapes mitochondrial activity and cellular differentiation

abstract: Turbulence is chaotic, yet its fluctuations follow a structured, nonequilibrium energy cascade unconstrained by the equilibrium theorems that limit passive energy extraction from molecular gases. Here, we introduce turbulence shelters: hollow shells with a single aperture that filter eddies by scale, sustaining gradients in fluctuation intensity that drive directional particle transport despite zero mean fluid flux. Across three orders of magnitude in size, shelters establish particle concentration contrasts between their interior and the surrounding flow, with selectivity controlled by particle geometry, inertia, thermal fluctuations, and electrostatic forces. At the microscale, shelters discriminate particles differing by tens of nanometers independently of material composition. These results establish a design principle for selective filtration: Geometry that compartmentalizes turbulent fluctuations can harness ambient eddies to direct particle transport.
title: Quiet within, chaos without: Turbulence shelters drive selective particle capture and release

abstract: Wernicke's area in the posterior temporal lobe is classically defined by its role in speech comprehension, yet a paradox remains: Why does damage here also profoundly impair speech production? Using direct human brain recordings, cortical stimulation, and lesion analysis, we found that this region is not solely for perception. A discrete subzone within Wernicke's area, the left posterior superior temporal gyrus (lpSTG), becomes active before speech, is causally necessary for speech production, and codes features of whole upcoming words rather than low-level acoustics or articulatory information. Its neural activity is distinct from the auditory-feedback responses nearby and can decode intended speech in people with paralysis. Thus, while Wernicke's area is a key part of auditory cortex, it contains a dedicated subregion for speech generation.
title: A neural code for generative speech production in human Wernicke’s area

abstract: Ultrasound imaging relies on soft interfaces that transmit sound efficiently between a device and the body. Conventional gel couplants provide low acoustic loss but contain mobile liquid phases that can dry, flow, or leach during extended use. By contrast, mobile phase-free elastomers are more stable but generally attenuate megahertz ultrasound strongly, limiting their use as couplants. We report an interpenetrating bottlebrush elastomer molecularly designed to overcome this trade-off. A densely grafted backbone lowers the shear modulus without increasing shear loss, whereas well-packed sidechains reduce bulk compressibility, jointly suppressing acoustic attenuation in a soft elastomer. The resulting elastomer combines soft tissue-like mechanics with low-loss acoustics, providing a durable couplant for soft ultrasonic interfaces.
title: Interpenetrating bottlebrush elastomer for low-loss soft ultrasonic interfaces

abstract: Atmospheric nitrogen (N) deposition is a critical nutrient source for marine ecosystems, but its organic nitrogen (ON) component remains poorly quantified. We measured ON in marine aerosols collected during 21 research cruises transecting multiple ocean basins and both hemispheric high latitudes. We used these observations to constrain and evaluate an atmospheric chemistry model with updated ON sources and sinks, enabling global mapping of ON deposition. The model estimated annual ON deposition to oceans at 12.8 (4.0 to 22.7) teragrams of nitrogen per year (Tg N year −1 ), contributing 27% (11 to 40%) of total N deposition. Marine emissions supply 3.9 (0.7 to 6.9) Tg N year −1 (30%) of deposited ON, while terrestrial sources contribute 8.9 (3.3 to 15.7) Tg N year −1 (70%). In N-limited regions such as the central Atlantic and Indonesian seas, ON accounts for ~50% of total N deposition.
title: Atmospheric organic nitrogen is a major nutrient source to global oceans

abstract: Light carries angular momentum in two forms: spin, associated with polarization, and orbital, associated with helical wavefronts. Whereas spin angular momentum underlies well-known atomic selection rules, the role of orbital angular momentum (OAM) in light-matter interaction continues to be discussed in the literature. In this work, we investigate OAM transfer from a vortex laser beam to a trapped-ion quantum rotor using rotational sidebands of the electric quadrupole transition of 40 Ca + . We directly observe coherent transfer of optical OAM into quantized rotation and identify distinct selection rules for different rotational sidebands. This observation provides experimental evidence for a scale-dependent separation of angular momentum transfer pathways in light-matter interactions. Further, our work elucidates the previously reported modified selection rules in trapped-ion experiments, establishing a unified framework for twisted light–matter interactions.
title: Angular momentum transfer from an optical vortex to an atomic rotor

abstract: The soft lattice that enables the exceptional performance of halide perovskites inherently compromises their operational stability. Here, we show that soft-lattice perovskites can be stabilized through elastic-field reorganization induced by rigid nanodiamond inclusions. Their inclusion enabled efficient bulk-to-boundary load transfer, redistributing and dissipating internal elastic fields at grain boundaries rather than allowing their accumulation within the crystal interior. Suppression of intergranular sliding constrained lattice deformation and mitigated defect generation during prolonged operation. Devices based on the stabilized perovskites with an area of 0.09 square centimeters achieved a certified power conversion efficiency of 27.6%, and minimodules with an area of 16.1 square centimeters achieved 24.3%. These devices retained 80% of their initial PCE after 5000 hours of maximum power point operation at 85°C and 98% after 5000 hours of dynamically varying light-intensity day-night cycling.
title: Elastic-field reorganization stabilizes soft-lattice perovskites for durable solar cells

abstract: The relaxin receptor RXFP1 is a therapeutic target owing to its potential benefits in the treatment of fibrosis and heart failure. Protein and small-molecule agonists are currently in midstage clinical trials for various forms of heart disease. In this work, we present three cryo–electron microscopy structures of RXFP1: ligand-free, bound to the native agonist relaxin-2, and bound to the small-molecule drug candidate AZD5462. These structures reveal that relaxin-2 engages the receptor’s ectodomain, whereas AZD5462 binds to the transmembrane domain. Together with hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry, we show that relaxin-2 induces reorganization of the linker domain into a helical secondary structure. By contrast, AZD5462 stabilizes an active conformation through a distinct set of conformational rearrangements. Altogether, our findings define divergent activation mechanisms for protein and small-molecule agonists of RXFP1.
title: Divergent activation of the RXFP1 relaxin receptor by protein and small-molecule agonists

abstract: Polycyclic frameworks are prevalent in natural products and bioactive molecules, yet their efficient enantioselective synthesis remains a longstanding challenge.
